Provided that if the confession is made after the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, coercion or promise has, in the opinion of the Court, been fully removed, it is relevant:
Provided further that if such a confession is otherwise relevant, it does not become irrelevant merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy, or in consequence of a deception practised on the accused person for the purpose of obtaining it, or when he was drunk, or because it was made in answer to questions which he need not have answered, whatever may have been the form of those questions, or because he was not warned that he was not bound to make such confession, and that evidence of it might be given against him.

breakdown.plain_summary: A confession is irrelevant in a criminal case if the Court finds it was caused by inducement, threat, coercion, or promise connected to the charge, coming from a person in authority, and substantial enough to give the accused reasonable grounds to believe confessing would bring an advantage or avoid harm. The first proviso restores relevance if the tainting impression was later fully removed before the confession was made. The second proviso is a list of things that do NOT by themselves taint a confession: a promise of secrecy, deception used to obtain it, drunkenness, answering questions one need not have answered, or the absence of a warning that the accused was not bound to speak.
essential_elements: The confession must be shown, in the Court's view, to have been caused by inducement, threat, coercion, or promise referencing the charge.
That inducement, threat, coercion, or promise must proceed from a person in authority.
It must be sufficient to give the accused reasonable grounds to believe confessing would secure a temporal advantage or avoid a temporal evil in relation to the proceedings.
Proviso 1: if the tainting impression was, in the Court's opinion, fully removed before the confession, the confession is relevant.
Proviso 2: a confession otherwise relevant does not become irrelevant merely because of a secrecy promise, deception, drunkenness, unnecessary questions answered, or absence of a warning.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section is the primary statutory filter for coerced or induced confessions in criminal trials -- the four-part test (inducement/threat/coercion/promise + reference to the charge + person in authority + reasonable grounds for temporal advantage/evil) must all be satisfied for the confession to be excluded, and the exclusion can still be cured under the first proviso.
breakdown.how_to_read: Run every contested confession through this section first: identify the specific inducement/threat/coercion/promise, confirm it came from a 'person in authority', and test whether the taint was removed before the confession was actually made -- the second proviso's list is a checklist of arguments that will NOT succeed in excluding a confession on their own.

sections.title: Confession to police officer
sections.raw_text:
23. (1) No confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence.
(2) No confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate shall be proved against him:
Provided that when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered, may be proved.

breakdown.plain_summary: Two absolute bars protect against unreliable police-extracted confessions: a confession made to a police officer can never be proved against the accused, and a confession made while in police custody can never be proved unless made in a Magistrate's immediate presence. The proviso carves out a narrow, separate exception -- the 'discovery' rule -- letting in only the part of a police-custody statement that distinctly relates to a fact actually discovered as a result of it.
essential_elements: Subsection (1): a confession made to a police officer is never provable against the accused.
Subsection (2): a confession made in police custody is not provable unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate.

Proviso: where a fact is discovered as a consequence of information given by an accused in police custody, so much of that information as distinctly relates to the discovered fact may be proved, whether or not it amounts to a confession.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso is a genuine exception, not a loophole for the whole statement -- only the portion of the information distinctly connected to what was actually discovered is admissible; the rest of any accompanying confession remains barred.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the constitutional-adjacent safeguard against coerced police confessions -- always check first whether the confession was to a police officer or in police custody, then separately test whether any part of it survives only through the narrow discovery-of-fact proviso.

sections.title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence
sections.raw_text:
24. When more persons than one are being tried jointly for the same offence, and a confession made by one of such persons affecting himself and some other of such persons is proved, the Court may take into consideration such confession as against such other person as well as against the person who makes such confession.
Explanation I.—“Offence”, as used in this section, includes the abetment of, or attempt to commit, the offence.
Explanation II.—A trial of more persons than one held in the absence of the accused who has absconded or who fails to comply with a proclamation issued under section 84 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 shall be deemed to be a joint trial for the purpose of this section.
Illustrations.
(a) A and B are jointly tried for the murder of C. It is proved that A said—“B and I murdered C”. The Court may consider the effect of this confession as against B.
(b) A is on his trial for the murder of C. There is evidence to show that C was murdered by A and B, and that B said—“A and I murdered C”. This statement may not be taken into consideration by the Court against A, as B is not being jointly tried.

breakdown.plain_summary: When two or more people are jointly tried for the same offence, one co-accused's proved confession that implicates both himself and the other can be weighed by the Court against that other person too -- not just against the confessor. Explanation I extends 'offence' to cover abetment and attempt. Explanation II deems a trial held in a proclaimed absconder's absence to still be a 'joint trial' for this purpose.
essential_elements: Two or more persons must be jointly tried for the same offence.
A confession by one of them, proved, must implicate both himself and the co-accused.
The Court may then consider that confession as evidence against the co-accused as well as the confessor.
Explanation I: 'offence' includes abetment of, or attempt to commit, the offence.
Explanation II: a trial held in the absence of an absconder under BNSS section 84 counts as a joint trial for this section.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Illustration (b) marks the boundary: if the co-accused is not actually being jointly tried (a separate trial), the other person's confession cannot be used against the absent party at all.
breakdown.how_to_read: The word 'jointly' is doing all the work -- confirm the co-accused are genuinely being tried together (or deemed so under Explanation II) before treating one's confession as usable, even circumstantially, against the other.

sections.title: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop
sections.raw_text: 25. Admissions are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted but they may operate as estoppels under the provisions hereinafter contained.

breakdown.plain_summary: An admission is not automatically decisive -- the Court can still weigh other evidence against it. But separately, an admission can trigger an estoppel, permanently barring the person who made it from later denying it, if the Adhiniyam's estoppel provisions are satisfied.
essential_elements: Admissions do not amount to conclusive proof of the matters they admit.
Admissions may nonetheless operate as an estoppel, but only under the estoppel provisions found elsewhere in the Adhiniyam.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Do not conflate the evidentiary weight of an admission (which remains rebuttable) with the separate, stricter doctrine of estoppel (which can permanently bar a party from resiling from what they said) -- the two operate on different legal tracks.
breakdown.how_to_read: Keep 'admission as evidence' and 'admission as estoppel' analytically separate: this section is the bridge telling you the second doctrine exists but is governed by its own dedicated provisions, not by the admissions sub-topic itself.

sections.title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant
sections.raw_text:
26. Statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, or who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the following cases, namely:—
Statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses
(a) when the statement is made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question. Such statements are relevant whether the person who made them was or was not, at the time when they were made, under expectation of death, and whatever may be the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question;
(b) when the statement was made by such person in the ordinary course of business, and in particular when it consists of any entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in the ordinary course of business, or in the discharge of professional duty; or of an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money, goods, securities or property of any kind; or of a document used in commerce written or signed by him; or of the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or signed by him;
(c) when the statement is against the pecuniary or proprietary interest of the person making it, or when, if true, it would expose him or would have exposed him to a criminal prosecution or to a suit for damages;
(d) when the statement gives the opinion of any such person, as to the existence of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest, of the existence of which, if it existed, he would have been likely to be aware, and when such statement was made before any controversy as to such right, custom or matter had arisen;
(e) when the statement relates to the existence of any relationship by blood, marriage or adoption between persons as to whose relationship by blood, marriage or adoption the person making the statement had special means of knowledge, and when the statement was made before the question in dispute was raised;
(f) when the statement relates to the existence of any relationship by blood, marriage or adoption between persons deceased, and is made in any will or deed relating to the affairs of the family to which any such deceased person belonged, or in any family pedigree, or upon any tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made, and when such statement was made before the question in dispute was raised;
(g) when the statement is contained in any deed, will or other document which relates to any such transaction as is specified in clause (a) of section 11;
(h) when the statement was made by a number of persons, and expressed feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A was murdered by B; or A dies of injuries received in a transaction in the course of which she was raped. The question is whether she was raped by B; or the question is, whether A was killed by B under such circumstances that a suit would lie against B by A's widow. Statements made by A as to the cause of his or her death, referring respectively to the murder, the rape and the actionable wrong under consideration, are relevant facts.
(b) The question is as to the date of A's birth. An entry in the diary of a deceased surgeon regularly kept in the course of business, stating that, on a given day he attended A's mother and delivered her of a son, is a relevant fact.
(c) The question is, whether A was in Nagpur on a given day. A statement in the diary of a deceased solicitor, regularly kept in the course of business, that on a given day the solicitor attended A at a place mentioned, in Nagpur, for the purpose of conferring with him upon specified business, is a relevant fact.
(d) The question is, whether a ship sailed from Mumbai harbour on a given day. A letter written by a deceased member of a merchant's firm by which she was chartered to their correspondents in Chennai, to whom the cargo was consigned, stating that the ship sailed on a given day from Mumbai port, is a relevant fact.
(e) The question is, whether rent was paid to A for certain land. A letter from A's deceased agent to A, saying that he had received the rent on A's account and held it at A's orders is a relevant fact.
(f) The question is, whether A and B were legally married. The statement of a deceased clergyman that he married them under such circumstances that the celebration would be a crime is relevant.
(g) The question is, whether A, a person who cannot be found, wrote a letter on a certain day. The fact that a letter written by him is dated on that day is relevant.
(h) The question is, what was the cause of the wreck of a ship. A protest made by the captain, whose attendance cannot be procured, is a relevant fact.
(i) The question is, whether a given road is a public way. A statement by A, a deceased headman of the village, that the road was public, is a relevant fact.
(j) The question is, what was the price of grain on a certain day in a particular market. A statement of the price, made by a deceased business person in the ordinary course of his business, is a relevant fact.
(k) The question is, whether A, who is dead, was the father of B. A statement by A that B was his son, is a relevant fact.
(l) The question is, what was the date of the birth of A. A letter from A's deceased father to a friend, announcing the birth of A on a given day, is a relevant fact.
(m) The question is, whether, and when, A and B were married. An entry in a memorandum book by C, the deceased father of B, of his daughter's marriage with A on a given date, is a relevant fact.
(n) A sues B for a libel expressed in a painted caricature exposed in a shop window. The question is as to the similarity of the caricature and its libellous character. The remarks of a crowd of spectators on these points may be proved.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section is the Adhiniyam's main gateway for hearsay from unavailable declarants -- persons dead, untraceable, incapacitated, or whose attendance would cost unreasonable delay or expense. Their statements become relevant facts in eight defined categories: (a) dying declarations about the cause of death; (b) ordinary-course-of-business entries and commercial documents; (c) statements against the maker's own pecuniary, proprietary, or penal interest; (d) opinions on public rights/customs made before any controversy arose; (e) statements on blood/marriage/adoption relationships made by someone with special knowledge, before any dispute arose; (f) similar relationship statements found in wills, pedigrees, tombstones, or family portraits; (g) statements in deeds/wills relating to transactions under section 11(a); and (h) collective statements of feeling or impression by a group of people.
essential_elements: The declarant must be dead, untraceable, incapable of giving evidence, or unreasonably difficult/expensive to produce.
The statement must fall within one of clauses (a) to (h) -- an exhaustive list of categories.
Clause (a) dying declarations require no expectation-of-death and apply in any type of proceeding, not just homicide trials.
Clauses (d) and (e) both require the statement to predate the rise of any controversy or dispute on the matter.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (a)'s dying declaration exception is notably broader than the general common-law notion -- it applies regardless of the declarant's expectation of death and regardless of whether the proceeding is criminal or civil.
The eight clauses are the exclusive gateways; a statement by an unavailable person that does not fit any of (a) to (h) remains inadmissible under this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: Work through the clauses like a checklist whenever a witness is unavailable: first confirm the unavailability ground, then match the statement's content precisely to one of the eight categories -- dying declarations (a) and business-record entries (b) are the two most frequently invoked in practice.

sections.title: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated
sections.raw_text:
27. Evidence given by a witness in a judicial proceeding, or before any person authorised by law to take it, is relevant for the purpose of proving, in a subsequent judicial proceeding, or in a later stage of the same judicial proceeding, the truth of the facts which it states, when the witness is dead or cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence, or is kept out of the way by the adverse party, or if his presence cannot be obtained without an amount of delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, the Court considers unreasonable:
Provided that the proceeding was between the same parties or their representatives in interest; that the adverse party in the first proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross-examine and the questions in issue were substantially the same in the first as in the second proceeding.
Explanation.—A criminal trial or inquiry shall be deemed to be a proceeding between the prosecutor and the accused within the meaning of this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: Prior testimony from an earlier judicial proceeding (or a stage of the same proceeding) can be used to prove the truth of what it states in a later proceeding, if the witness is now dead, untraceable, incapacitated, deliberately kept away by the adverse party, or unreasonably costly/delayed to produce. Three conditions in the proviso must all be met: same parties (or their privies), the adverse party had the right and opportunity to cross-examine the first time, and the issues were substantially the same in both proceedings.
essential_elements: The evidence must have been given by a witness in a judicial proceeding, or before a person legally authorised to take evidence.
The witness must now be dead, untraceable, incapable of testifying, kept away by the adverse party, or unreasonably difficult/costly to produce.
Proviso condition 1: the two proceedings must be between the same parties or their representatives in interest.
Proviso condition 2: the adverse party in the earlier proceeding must have had the right and opportunity to cross-examine.
Proviso condition 3: the questions in issue must have been substantially the same in both proceedings.
Explanation: a criminal trial or inquiry is deemed a proceeding between prosecutor and accused for this section's purposes.
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Kept out of the way by the adverse party' is itself a distinct unavailability ground -- a party cannot benefit from their own act of hiding a witness to block prior testimony from a first proceeding from being used.
All three proviso conditions are cumulative, not alternative; missing any one defeats reliance on this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the mechanism for carrying forward testimony across proceedings (e.g. from committal to trial, or between related civil suits) -- always verify the cross-examination opportunity and substantial-sameness-of-issues conditions before assuming prior testimony can simply be read in.

sections.title: Entries in books of account when relevant
sections.raw_text:
28. Entries in the books of account, including those maintained in an electronic form, regularly kept in the course of business are relevant whenever they refer to a matter into which the Court has to inquire, but such statements shall not alone be sufficient evidence to charge any person with liability.
Illustration.
A sues B for one thousand rupees, and shows entries in his account books showing B to be indebted to him to this amount. The entries are relevant, but are not sufficient, without other evidence, to prove the debt.

breakdown.plain_summary: Regularly-kept business account entries, including electronic ones, are relevant to any matter the Court is inquiring into. But they are never enough on their own to fix liability on a person -- some independent corroborating evidence is always required before a court can act on the entries alone.
essential_elements: Entries must be in books of account, which may be maintained in electronic form.
The entries must be regularly kept in the course of business.
They are relevant whenever they refer to a matter under the Court's inquiry.
Standing alone, such entries are never sufficient evidence to charge any person with liability -- corroboration is required.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The illustration is the working rule in every debt-recovery suit relying on account books: relevance is not the same as sufficiency, and a plaintiff must bring something more than their own ledger to prove the debt.
breakdown.how_to_read: Never treat a party's own account-book entries as self-proving -- they clear the relevance bar automatically but always need independent corroboration to actually carry the burden of proof.

sections.title: Relevancy of entry in public record or an electronic record made in performance of duty
sections.raw_text: 29. An entry in any public or other official book, register or record or an electronic record, stating a fact in issue or relevant fact, and made by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty, or by any other person in performance of a duty specially enjoined by the law of the country in which such book, register or record or an electronic record, is kept, is itself a relevant fact.

breakdown.plain_summary: An entry in an official book, register, record, or electronic record is itself a relevant fact if it states a fact in issue or relevant fact, and was made either by a public servant in the discharge of official duty, or by anyone else performing a duty that the law specifically requires of them.
essential_elements: The entry must be in a public or official book, register, record, or electronic record.
It must state a fact in issue or a relevant fact.
It must have been made by a public servant in the discharge of official duty, or by another person performing a legally-enjoined duty.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section covers electronic official records on the same footing as paper ones, reflecting the Adhiniyam's general modernisation of the evidence framework for digital records.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the standard route for admitting official records -- land registers, birth/death registers, government electronic databases -- as relevant facts without needing to call the recording official as a witness.

sections.title: Relevancy of statements in maps, charts and plans
sections.raw_text: 30. Statements of facts in issue or relevant facts, made in published maps or charts generally offered for public sale, or in maps or plans made under the authority of the Central Government or any State Government, as to matters usually represented or stated in such maps, charts or plans, are themselves relevant facts.

breakdown.plain_summary: Statements found in publicly-sold maps or charts, or in maps/plans made under Central or State Government authority, are themselves relevant facts -- but only as to the kind of matters such maps, charts, or plans ordinarily represent or state.
essential_elements: The statement must appear in a published map or chart generally offered for public sale, or a map/plan made under Central or State Government authority.
The statement must concern a fact in issue or relevant fact.
The statement must be of a kind usually represented or stated in such maps, charts, or plans.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The relevance is limited to the map's customary subject matter -- a government survey map is relevant as to boundaries or terrain it typically depicts, not for unrelated annotations that happen to appear on it.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful for boundary and land-related disputes -- official survey maps or widely-sold published maps can be relied on directly for the facts they typically depict, without separately proving the mapmaker's personal knowledge.

sections.title: Relevancy of statement as to fact of public nature contained in certain Acts or notifications
sections.raw_text: 31. When the Court has to form an opinion as to the existence of any fact of a public nature, any statement of it, made in a recital contained in any Central Act or State Act or in a Central Government or State Government notification appearing in the respective Official Gazette or in any printed paper or in electronic or digital form purporting to be such Gazette, is a relevant fact.

breakdown.plain_summary: When the Court must decide whether a fact of a public nature exists, a recital of that fact in a Central or State Act, or in a government notification published in the Official Gazette (in print or in electronic/digital form), is itself relevant evidence of the fact.
essential_elements: The Court must be forming an opinion on the existence of a fact of a public nature.
The statement must be a recital in a Central Act, State Act, or a Government notification.
The notification must appear in the Official Gazette, whether in print or in electronic/digital form purporting to be such Gazette.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section covers digital/electronic Gazette copies on the same footing as print ones, so long as they purport to be the Official Gazette.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section to establish facts of public nature (like the creation of an administrative division or the appointment of an authority) directly from the Gazette recital, without needing further proof of the underlying fact.

sections.title: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form
sections.raw_text: 32. When the Court has to form an opinion as to a law of any country, any statement of such law contained in a book purporting to be printed or published including in electronic or digital form under the authority of the Government of such country and to contain any such law, and any report of a ruling of the Courts of such country contained in a book including in electronic or digital form purporting to be a report of such rulings, is relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: When the Court needs to determine the content of a foreign country's law, it may rely on a book (print or electronic/digital) purporting to be published under that country's government authority and to contain that law, and on law reports (print or electronic) purporting to report that country's court rulings.
essential_elements: The Court must be forming an opinion as to the law of some country.
The book must purport to be printed or published, including electronically, under that country's government authority and to contain the law in question.
Reports of that country's court rulings, in a book purporting to report such rulings (print or electronic), are likewise relevant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The section relies on the book's or report's purported authority/authenticity on its face -- it does not require independently proving the foreign legislature enacted the law as printed.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the standard route for proving foreign law in Indian courts -- authoritative published compilations and law reports substitute for calling a foreign-law expert every time.

sections.title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers
sections.raw_text: 33. When any statement of which evidence is given forms part of a longer statement, or of a conversation or part of an isolated document, or is contained in a document which forms part of a book, or is contained in part of electronic record or of a connected series of letters or papers, evidence shall be given of so much and no more of the statement, conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers as the Court considers necessary in that particular case to the full understanding of the nature and effect of the statement, and of the circumstances under which it was made.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the anti-cherry-picking rule: when only part of a larger statement, conversation, document, electronic record, book, or series of connected letters/papers is put in evidence, the Court can require as much more of it to be proved as is necessary to fully understand the nature, effect, and context of the part relied upon.
essential_elements: The statement in evidence must form part of a longer statement, conversation, document, book, electronic record, or connected series of letters/papers.
The Court decides how much of the larger whole is necessary for full understanding of the nature and effect of the statement and the circumstances of its making.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a Court-controlled, case-by-case standard -- there is no fixed proportion; the test is full understanding of the excerpted statement's nature, effect, and circumstances.
breakdown.how_to_read: Invoke this section whenever an opposing party introduces an out-of-context excerpt -- it entitles you to insist on the surrounding context being placed in evidence too.

sections.title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial
sections.raw_text: 34. The existence of any judgment, order or decree which by law prevents any Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, is a relevant fact when the question is whether such Court ought to take cognizance of such suit or to hold such trial.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a prior judgment, order, or decree legally bars a Court from taking up a suit or holding a trial (for instance, on grounds like res judicata or double jeopardy), the existence of that prior judgment is itself a relevant fact whenever the question is whether the Court should take cognizance of the later suit or hold the later trial.
essential_elements: There must exist a judgment, order, or decree that, by law, bars a Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial.
Its existence is relevant when the question before the Court is whether it ought to take cognizance of that suit or hold that trial.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section only makes the prior judgment's existence relevant to the cognizance/bar question -- the substantive law of when a prior judgment actually operates as a bar (res judicata, autrefois acquit/convict, etc.) lies outside the Adhiniyam itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section as the evidentiary hook for raising a bar to a second suit or trial -- it lets the prior judgment's existence in be proved, while the actual bar doctrine comes from the relevant procedural code.

sections.title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

breakdown.plain_summary: Final judgments from probate, matrimonial, admiralty, or insolvency proceedings that fix a person's legal character (e.g. declaring someone an heir, a divorced spouse, or an insolvent), or their absolute entitlement to a specific thing, are relevant -- and, under subsection (2), conclusive proof (not merely rebuttable) of exactly when that legal character or entitlement accrued, was declared, or ceased, as fixed by the judgment itself.
essential_elements: The judgment, order, or decree must be final and from a competent Court or Tribunal.
It must be in probate, matrimonial, admiralty, or insolvency jurisdiction.
It must confer, take away, or declare a legal character, or declare an absolute (not merely as-against-a-specified-person) entitlement to a specific thing.

Subsection (2): such a judgment is conclusive proof of the precise timing of the conferral, declaration, cessation, or ownership it states -- this is a stronger evidentiary status than ordinary relevance.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is one of the rare instances in the Adhiniyam where a judgment is elevated to 'conclusive proof' rather than merely relevant, rebuttable evidence -- it applies strictly to the four listed jurisdictions and to judgments operating in rem (absolutely), not inter partes.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish 'absolutely' (in rem, binding the world) from judgments that only bind named parties -- only the former, from these four jurisdictions, gets the conclusive-proof status under subsection (2); everything else falls to section 36 or 37 instead.

sections.title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35
sections.raw_text:
36. Judgments, orders or decrees other than those mentioned in section 35 are relevant if they relate to matters of a public nature relevant to the enquiry; but such judgments, orders or decrees are not conclusive proof of that which they state.
Illustration.
A sues B for trespass on his land. B alleges the existence of a public right of way over the land, which A denies. The existence of a decree in favour of the defendant, in a suit by A against C for a trespass on the same land, in which C alleged the existence of the same right of way, is relevant, but it is not conclusive proof that the right of way exists.

breakdown.plain_summary: Judgments outside section 35's four special jurisdictions are still relevant if they concern matters of a public nature bearing on the inquiry -- but unlike section 35 judgments, they are never conclusive; they remain ordinary, rebuttable evidence of what they state.
essential_elements: The judgment, order, or decree must not be one of the section 35 category.
It must relate to a matter of a public nature relevant to the current enquiry.
Such a judgment is relevant, but is not conclusive proof of the matters it states.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The illustration shows the practical effect: a prior decree recognising a public right of way in a different suit is admissible to support the same claim in a new suit, but the new Court remains free to reach its own conclusion on the evidence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast directly with section 35: same broad category of 'judgment as evidence', but here the evidentiary weight is only relevance, never conclusiveness -- a crucial distinction to flag when arguing how much a prior judgment should count.

sections.title: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant
sections.raw_text:
37. Judgments or orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36, are irrelevant, unless the existence of such judgment, order or decree is a fact in issue, or is relevant under some other provision of this Adhiniyam.
Illustrations.
(a) A and B separately sue C for a libel which reflects upon each of them. C in each case says that the matter alleged to be libellous is true, and the circumstances are such that it is probably true in each case, or in neither. A obtains a decree against C for damages on the ground that C failed to make out his justification. The fact is irrelevant as between B and C.
(b) A prosecutes B for stealing a cow from him. B is convicted. A afterwards sues C for the cow, which B had sold to him before his conviction. As between A and C, the judgment against B is irrelevant.
(c) A has obtained a decree for the possession of land against B. C, B's son, murders A in consequence. The existence of the judgment is relevant, as showing motive for a crime.
(d) A is charged with theft and with having been previously convicted of theft. The previous conviction is relevant as a fact in issue.
(e) A is tried for the murder of B. The fact that B prosecuted A for libel and that A was convicted and sentenced is relevant under section 6 as showing the motive for the fact in issue.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the residual, default-exclusion rule: any judgment, order, or decree that does not fall under sections 34, 35, or 36 is irrelevant, unless its existence is itself a fact in issue or is made relevant by some other provision of the Adhiniyam (such as section 6's motive/preparation/conduct rule).
essential_elements: The judgment, order, or decree must not fall within sections 34, 35, or 36.
Default position: such a judgment is irrelevant.
Exception: relevant if its existence is itself a fact in issue.
Exception: relevant if made relevant under any other provision of the Adhiniyam.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Illustrations (c) and (e) show the most common escape route in practice: a judgment irrelevant on its own terms can still come in through section 6, if it shows motive for the fact in issue.
Illustrations (a) and (b) show the default bar operating -- a judgment against one party does not bind or even inform a case against a different party absent one of the listed exceptions.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this section as the closing default rule for the whole judgments sub-topic: if a judgment doesn't fit sections 34-36, it is presumptively out, and the only way back in is through 'fact in issue' status or another specific relevancy provision like section 6.

sections.title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved
sections.raw_text: 38. Any party to a suit or other proceeding may show that any judgment, order or decree which is relevant under section 34, 35 or 36, and which has been proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a Court not competent to deliver it, or was obtained by fraud or collusion.

breakdown.plain_summary: Even a judgment that is relevant (and in section 35's case, otherwise conclusive) under sections 34, 35, or 36 can be attacked: any party may show that the Court that delivered it lacked competence to do so, or that it was obtained through fraud or collusion between the parties to that earlier proceeding.
essential_elements: The judgment, order, or decree must be one relevant under section 34, 35, or 36.
It must have been proved by the adverse party.
The party against whom it is used may show either that the delivering Court was not competent, or that the judgment was obtained by fraud or collusion.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the safety valve against sections 34-36's otherwise strong evidentiary effect (including section 35's conclusive proof) -- competence and fraud/collusion attacks are always open, no matter how conclusive the judgment would otherwise be.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always keep this section in reserve when facing an adverse judgment relied on under sections 34-36 -- even section 35's 'conclusive proof' status yields to a successful showing of incompetent Court or fraud/collusion in obtaining it.

sections.title: Opinions of experts
sections.raw_text:
39. (1) When the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law or of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts and such persons are called experts.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether the death of A was caused by poison. The opinions of experts as to the symptoms produced by the poison by which A is supposed to have died, are relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A, at the time of doing a certain act, was, by reason of unsoundness of mind, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he was doing what was either wrong or contrary to law. The opinions of experts upon the question whether the symptoms exhibited by A commonly show unsoundness of mind, and whether such unsoundness of mind usually renders persons incapable of knowing the nature of the acts which they do, or of knowing that what they do is either wrong or contrary to law, are relevant.
(c) The question is, whether a certain document was written by A. Another document is produced which is proved or admitted to have been written by A. The opinions of experts on the question whether the two documents were written by the same person or by different persons, are relevant.
(2) When in a proceeding, the court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to any information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, is a relevant fact.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section opens the opinion-evidence chapter. Ordinarily a witness may only testify to facts, not opinions -- but when the Court must decide a point of foreign law, science, art, or any other specialised field, or the identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of specially skilled persons (experts) on that point become relevant. Subsection (2) extends 'expert' status specifically to the statutory Examiner of Electronic Evidence for opinions on computer/electronic/digital information.
essential_elements: The Court must be forming an opinion on a point of foreign law, science, art, or any other field, or on identity of handwriting or finger impressions.
The opinion must be that of a person specially skilled in the relevant subject -- an expert.
Subsection (2): for electronic/digital information matters, the Examiner of Electronic Evidence under the IT Act, 2000 is deemed an expert.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section is the statutory exception to the general rule against opinion evidence -- it does not make every opinion relevant, only expert opinion within the listed specialised categories.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the gateway provision for the entire expert-witness practice -- forensic, medical, handwriting, and digital-forensic testimony all trace their relevance back to this section; always confirm the witness's special skill matches the specific field in question.

sections.title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts
sections.raw_text:
40. Facts, not otherwise relevant, are relevant if they support or are inconsistent with the opinions of experts, when such opinions are relevant.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A was poisoned by a certain poison. The fact that other persons, who were poisoned by that poison, exhibited certain symptoms which experts affirm or deny to be the symptoms of that poison, is relevant.
(b) The question is, whether an obstruction to a harbour is caused by a certain sea-wall. The fact that other harbours similarly situated in other respects, but where there were no such sea-walls, began to be obstructed at about the same time, is relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: Facts that would otherwise have no independent relevance become relevant if they either support or contradict an expert opinion that is itself relevant under section 39 -- letting parties test or corroborate expert testimony with comparative real-world data.
essential_elements: The fact in question must not otherwise be relevant on its own.
It becomes relevant because it either supports or is inconsistent with a relevant expert opinion.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a companion, evidence-testing provision to section 39 -- it only operates where an expert opinion is already relevant; it does not independently create relevance for comparative facts in the absence of expert opinion evidence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section to bring in comparative or corroborative data points (e.g. how other similarly-poisoned persons reacted, or how comparable harbours behaved) to strengthen or challenge an expert's opinion already before the Court.

sections.title: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant
sections.raw_text:
41. (1) When the Court has to form an opinion as to the person by whom any document was written or signed, the opinion of any person acquainted with the handwriting of the person by whom it is supposed to be written or signed that it was or was not written or signed by that person, is a relevant fact.
Explanation.—A person is said to be acquainted with the handwriting of another person when he has seen that person write, or when he has received documents purporting to be written by that person in answer to documents written by himself or under his authority and addressed to that person, or when, in the ordinary course of business, documents purporting to be written by that person have been habitually submitted to him.
Illustration.
The question is, whether a given letter is in the handwriting of A, a merchant in Itanagar. B is a merchant in Bengaluru, who has written letters addressed to A and received letters purporting to be written by him. C, is B's clerk whose duty it was to examine and file B's correspondence. D is B's broker, to whom B habitually submitted the letters purporting to be written by A for the purpose of advising him thereon. The opinions of B, C and D on the question whether the letter is in the handwriting of A are relevant, though neither B, C nor D ever saw A write.
(2) When the Court has to form an opinion as to the electronic signature of any person, the opinion of the Certifying Authority which has issued the Electronic Signature Certificate is a relevant fact.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a specific, lay-witness route to identifying a document's author -- someone who is 'acquainted' with a person's handwriting (in any of three ways defined by the Explanation) can give a relevant opinion on whether they wrote or signed a document, without needing to be a handwriting expert. Subsection (2) is the digital equivalent: for electronic signatures, the Certifying Authority that issued the Electronic Signature Certificate gives the relevant opinion.
essential_elements: The Court must be forming an opinion on who wrote or signed a document.

The opinion-giver must be 'acquainted with the handwriting' as defined by the Explanation -- having seen the person write, having corresponded with them, or having habitually received their documents in the ordinary course of business.
For electronic signatures, the relevant opinion is that of the Certifying Authority that issued the Electronic Signature Certificate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is distinct from section 39's expert-opinion route -- the illustration shows that none of B, C, or D ever saw A write, yet their opinions are still relevant because they satisfy one of the Explanation's three alternative bases for 'acquaintance'.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the everyday route to proving authorship of a letter or signature without engaging a forensic handwriting expert -- test any proposed witness against the Explanation's three routes to 'acquaintance' before relying on their opinion.

sections.title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant
sections.raw_text:
42. When the Court has to form an opinion as to the existence of any general custom or right, the opinions, as to the existence of such custom or right, of persons who would be likely to know of its existence if it existed, are relevant.
Explanation.—The expression “general custom or right” includes customs or rights common to any considerable class of persons.
Illustration.
The right of the villagers of a particular village to use the water of a particular well is a general right within the meaning of this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a custom or right shared by a considerable class of persons is in question, the opinions of people who would likely know about it if it existed are relevant -- a practical route to proving customs that are, by nature, rarely documented formally.
essential_elements: The Court must be forming an opinion on the existence of a general custom or right.
The opinion-giver must be someone who would likely know of the custom or right's existence, if it existed.
Explanation: 'general custom or right' covers customs or rights common to any considerable class of persons.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Relevance turns on the witness's likely proximity to knowledge of the custom, not on any formal qualification -- unlike the expert-opinion route under section 39.
breakdown.how_to_read: Commonly invoked in village/community rights disputes (grazing rights, water rights, rights of way) where no documentary record exists -- the witness's community positioning, not credentials, is what establishes relevance here.

sections.title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant
sections.raw_text:
43. When the Court has to form an opinion as to—
(i) the usages and tenets of any body of men or family;
(ii) the constitution and governance of any religious or charitable foundation; or
(iii) the meaning of words or terms used in particular districts or by particular classes of people,
the opinions of persons having special means of knowledge thereon, are relevant facts.

breakdown.plain_summary: Extends the opinion-evidence principle to three further specialised categories: the customs/beliefs of a group or family, the internal governance of a religious or charitable institution, and local or class-specific meanings of words or terms -- in each case, the opinion of someone with special means of knowledge on the point is relevant.
essential_elements: The opinion must concern one of three listed categories: (i) usages/tenets of a body of men or family, (ii) constitution/governance of a religious or charitable foundation, or (iii) local/class-specific meaning of words or terms.
The opinion-giver must have special means of knowledge on that specific point.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section is narrower than section 39's general expert-opinion rule -- it applies only to the three specifically enumerated categories, each requiring the more modest threshold of 'special means of knowledge' rather than formal expert skill.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful in disputes over religious trust administration, community customary practice, or regional/dialectal word meanings -- confirm the witness's special means of knowledge is tied to the specific category invoked.

sections.title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant
sections.raw_text:
44. When the Court has to form an opinion as to the relationship of one person to another, the opinion, expressed by conduct, as to the existence of such relationship, of any person who, as a member of the family or otherwise, has special means of knowledge on the subject, is a relevant fact:
Provided that such opinion shall not be sufficient to prove a marriage in proceedings under the Divorce Act, 1869, or in prosecution under sections 82 and 84 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A and B were married. The fact that they were usually received and treated by their friends as husband and wife, is relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A was the legitimate son of B. The fact that A was always treated as such by members of the family, is relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a family relationship (marriage, parentage, etc.) is in question, the conduct-expressed opinion of someone with special means of knowledge -- typically a family member -- is relevant, as shown by the illustrations' 'usually treated as' pattern. But the proviso caps this: such opinion evidence alone cannot suffice to prove a marriage in Divorce Act proceedings, or in prosecutions under BNS sections 82 (bigamy-type offence) and 84 (marriage by deception/without lawful marriage).
essential_elements: The Court must be forming an opinion on the relationship of one person to another.
The relevant opinion is one expressed through conduct, by a person with special means of knowledge (typically a family member).
Proviso: such opinion evidence is not, by itself, sufficient to prove a marriage in Divorce Act proceedings or in BNS sections 82/84 prosecutions -- stricter proof is required there.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso is a deliberate heightened-proof carve-out for marriage-specific proceedings -- conduct-based 'reputation of marriage' evidence that would suffice for an ordinary civil relationship question is not enough on its own in those specific contexts.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish general relationship questions (where conduct-based family opinion suffices) from marriage validity in Divorce Act or BNS 82/84 proceedings (where this section's proviso demands more than reputation-style evidence).

sections.title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant
sections.raw_text:
45. Whenever the opinion of any living person is relevant, the grounds on which such opinion is based are also relevant.
Illustration.
An expert may give an account of experiments performed by him for the purpose of forming his opinion.

breakdown.plain_summary: Wherever a living person's opinion is relevant under any of the preceding opinion-evidence sections, the reasoning and basis behind that opinion is also relevant -- letting the Court and opposing parties test not just the conclusion but the methodology behind it.
essential_elements: The opinion in question must be that of a living person and must itself be relevant (under sections 39 to 44).
The grounds on which that opinion is based are then also relevant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the evidentiary hook for cross-examining experts and opinion witnesses on their methodology -- without it, only the bare conclusion, not its foundation, would be fair game.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always pair any admitted opinion evidence with an inquiry into its grounds under this section -- it is the primary route to testing an expert's methodology, data, or reasoning in cross-examination.

sections.title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant
sections.raw_text: 46. In civil cases the fact that the character of any person concerned is such as to render probable or improbable any conduct imputed to him, is irrelevant, except in so far as such character appears from facts otherwise relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: In civil litigation, a person's character cannot be used to argue that conduct imputed to them is more or less probable -- character evidence for this purpose is barred, unless the character happens to emerge from facts that are independently relevant on some other ground.
essential_elements: Applies in civil cases.
General rule: a person's character, offered to show that imputed conduct is probable or improbable, is irrelevant.
Exception: relevant only insofar as the character appears from facts that are otherwise relevant anyway.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Contrast sharply with section 47 (criminal cases): civil cases exclude character evidence of this kind almost entirely, while criminal cases specifically admit good character for the accused.
breakdown.how_to_read: Do not attempt to introduce a civil litigant's general character or reputation to argue they probably did or didn't do the imputed act -- it is barred unless it rides in through independently relevant facts.

sections.title: In criminal cases previous good character relevant
sections.raw_text: 47. In criminal proceedings the fact that the person accused is of a good character, is relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: Unlike the civil-case bar in section 46, an accused person's good character is affirmatively relevant in criminal proceedings -- a long-standing protection allowing the defence to put the accused's reputation before the Court.
essential_elements: Applies in criminal proceedings.
The fact that the accused is of good character is relevant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This relevance is one-directional at the defence's initiative -- section 49 governs when the prosecution may respond with bad-character evidence once good character has been put in issue.
breakdown.how_to_read: A standard defence tool -- but be aware that invoking it under section 47 opens the door to the prosecution's rebuttal under section 49's 'except in reply' clause.

sections.title: Evidence of character or previous sexual experience not relevant in certain cases
sections.raw_text: 48. In a prosecution for an offence under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77 or section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or for attempt to commit any such offence, where the question of consent is in issue, evidence of the character of the victim or of such person's previous sexual experience with any person shall not be relevant on the issue of such consent or the quality of consent.

breakdown.plain_summary: In prosecutions for the listed sexual-offence provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (and attempts to commit them) where consent is in issue, the victim's character or their previous sexual history with anyone is barred from being used as evidence on the question of consent or its quality -- a victim-protective exclusion rule.
essential_elements: Must be a prosecution under one of the specifically listed BNS sections (64-71, 74-78), or an attempt to commit such an offence.
The question of consent must be in issue.
Evidence of the victim's character, or of their previous sexual experience with any person, is not relevant on the question of consent or its quality.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a categorical exclusion, not merely a weight-limiting rule -- such evidence is inadmissible outright on the consent question, regardless of how probative a party might argue it to be.
breakdown.how_to_read: A critical protective provision in sexual-offence trials -- character and sexual-history evidence of the complainant cannot be used to argue consent, closing off a line of cross-examination that was historically misused to attack victim credibility.

sections.title: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply
sections.raw_text:
49. In criminal proceedings, the fact that the accused has a bad character, is irrelevant, unless evidence has been given that he has a good character, in which case it becomes relevant.
Explanation 1.—This section does not apply to cases in which the bad character of any person is itself a fact in issue.
Explanation 2.—A previous conviction is relevant as evidence of bad character.

breakdown.plain_summary: The accused's bad character is generally irrelevant in a criminal proceeding -- but the moment the defence puts good character in evidence under section 47, the door opens and bad character becomes relevant in reply. Explanation 1 clarifies this bar does not apply where bad character is itself a fact in issue. Explanation 2 confirms a previous conviction counts as evidence of bad character.
essential_elements: Default rule: the accused's bad character is irrelevant in criminal proceedings.
Exception: once evidence of the accused's good character has been given, bad character becomes relevant in reply.
Explanation 1: the section does not apply where bad character is itself a fact in issue.
Explanation 2: a previous conviction is relevant as evidence of bad character.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the direct counterpart to section 47 -- invoking good character is a calculated risk for the defence, since it is what triggers the prosecution's right to introduce bad-character evidence, including prior convictions under Explanation 2.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always advise that raising good character under section 47 is a door that swings both ways -- the prosecution's reply rights under this section, especially the prior-conviction route in Explanation 2, can outweigh the benefit of raising it.

sections.title: Character as affecting damages
sections.raw_text:
50. In civil cases, the fact that the character of any person is such as to affect the amount of damages which he ought to receive, is relevant.
Explanation.—In this section and sections 46, 47 and 49, the word “character” includes both reputation and disposition; but, except as provided in section 49, evidence may be given only of general reputation and general disposition, and not of particular acts by which reputation or disposition has been shown.

breakdown.plain_summary: In civil cases, a person's character is relevant if it bears on the quantum of damages they ought to receive. The Explanation is the unifying definitional provision for this entire character sub-topic: 'character' means both reputation and disposition, but -- except where section 49 permits otherwise (bad character in reply, including prior convictions) -- only general reputation and general disposition may be proved, never particular acts offered as illustrations of that reputation or disposition.
essential_elements: Applies in civil cases.
A person's character, insofar as it affects the amount of damages they ought to receive, is relevant.
Explanation: 'character' covers both reputation and disposition across sections 46, 47, 49 and 50.
Explanation: only general reputation and general disposition may be proved -- not particular acts -- except as section 49 separately allows.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation's particular-acts bar is the key practical limit across the entire character sub-topic -- even where character evidence is otherwise admissible, specific incident-by-incident proof is barred in favour of general reputation and disposition testimony only.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this Explanation as the closing definitional anchor for sections 46-50 as a whole -- it is what stops character evidence, wherever admissible, from turning into a trial about specific past incidents rather than general reputation.

sections.title: Fact judicially noticeable need not be proved
sections.raw_text: 51. No fact of which the Court will take judicial notice need be proved.

breakdown.plain_summary: A one-line rule: if a fact falls within the categories the Court is required (or entitled) to judicially notice, no party needs to lead evidence to prove it. Section 52 spells out exactly what those categories are.
essential_elements: The fact must be one of which the Court will take judicial notice (see section 52).
No further proof of that fact is required from any party.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short gateway provision -- read it together with section 52, which is the operative list. Section 51 just states the consequence: judicially noticeable facts are proof-free.

sections.title: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the operative list underlying section 51: twelve categories of fact (laws in force, treaties, legislative proceedings, Court seals, public office holders notified in the Gazette, recognised countries and flags, calendar/geographical divisions and notified holidays, India's territory, war-related events, the Court's own personnel, and road/sea traffic rules) that the Court must simply accept as true, no evidence needed. Subsection (2) lets the Court consult reference books for these and for general matters of history, literature, science, or art, and lets it decline to notice a fact until a party produces the reference material to support it.
essential_elements: Subsection (1) is a closed list of 12 categories (a) to (l) the Court MUST judicially notice.

Categories include: all laws in force (including extra-territorial ones), international treaties/agreements, legislative proceedings, Court/Tribunal seals, specified official seals, Gazette-notified public officeholders, recognised countries/flags, Gazette-notified calendar and holiday facts, India's territory, war-related facts, the Court's own officers/advocates, and road/sea traffic rules.

Subsection (2) additionally covers matters of public history, literature, science, or art -- but here the Court MAY (not must) resort to reference books, and may refuse to notice the fact until the requesting party produces supporting material.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The subsection (2) discretion is a genuine qualification: for general historical/literary/scientific/artistic facts (unlike the subsection (1) list), the Court can insist on documentary backup before noticing them.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat subsection (1) as a checklist -- if your fact fits one of (a) to (l), you can simply assert it without evidence. For anything broader (general history, science, art), be ready with a reference book or document, since subsection (2) lets the Court demand one.

sections.title: Facts admitted need not be proved
sections.raw_text:
53. No fact needs to be proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their agents agree to admit at the hearing, or which, before the hearing, they agree to admit by any writing under their hands, or which by any rule of pleading in force at the time they are deemed to have admitted by their pleadings:
Provided that the Court may, in its discretion, require the facts admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admissions.

breakdown.plain_summary: Facts the parties themselves agree are true -- whether admitted orally at the hearing, admitted in writing beforehand, or deemed admitted under pleading rules -- don't need separate proof. This closes Chapter III's proof-free trilogy alongside judicially noticed facts (sections 51-52): judicial notice and party admission are the two routes to skipping formal proof. The proviso is the safety valve -- the Court can still insist on independent proof if it doesn't trust the admission.
essential_elements: The fact must be admitted by the parties or their agents at the hearing, in signed writing before the hearing, or deemed admitted under applicable pleading rules.
Once admitted in one of these ways, no further proof of that fact is required.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Proviso: the Court retains discretion to require the admitted fact to be proved by other means anyway -- an admission does not bind the Court's fact-finding the way it binds the parties' pleading position.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pairs with sections 51-52 to complete the 'proof not required' trio for Chapter III. Practically, this is why well-drafted admissions in pleadings or joint statements can shrink a trial -- but never assume an admission is bulletproof; the proviso means a cautious Court can still demand evidence.

sections.title: Proof of facts by oral evidence
sections.raw_text: 54. All facts, except the contents of documents may be proved by oral evidence.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter IV (Oral Evidence) with the basic division of labour between oral and documentary proof: oral evidence can prove any fact except one thing -- what a document actually says. The contents of documents are proved by the document itself (subject to the documentary-evidence rules in Chapter V), not by a witness's oral account of what it contained.
essential_elements: Oral evidence is competent to prove any fact.
The sole carve-out: the contents of documents cannot be proved by oral evidence -- that is the domain of documentary evidence (Chapter V).
breakdown.how_to_read: A short bridging section: remember it mainly for the carve-out. If the fact you are trying to establish is literally what a document says, oral testimony about it is the wrong tool -- you need the document (or secondary evidence of it under the rules already covered).

sections.title: Oral evidence to be direct

breakdown.plain_summary: The hearsay-exclusion backbone of oral evidence: whatever a witness testifies to must come from their own first-hand perception, not something they were told. Seen facts need an eyewitness, heard facts need an earwitness, facts perceived by other senses need the person who perceived them that way, and opinions need the person who actually holds that opinion (and their grounds for it) -- not someone relaying it second-hand. Two practical safety valves follow: published expert treatises can substitute for a now-unavailable expert witness, and the Court can demand the actual physical object be produced for inspection instead of relying purely on a witness's description of it.
essential_elements: General rule: oral evidence must always be direct, i.e., first-hand.
Seen facts: testimony must come from a witness who says they personally saw it.
Heard facts: testimony must come from a witness who says they personally heard it.
Facts perceived by other senses/manners: testimony must come from the person who personally perceived it that way.
Opinions and their grounds: testimony must come from the person who actually holds that opinion.
exceptions_and_qualifications: First proviso: a dead, untraceable, incapacitated, or unreasonably-difficult-to-call expert's opinion can be proved by producing their published treatise instead of live testimony.
Second proviso: for any material thing other than a document, the Court may, at its discretion, require the thing itself to be produced for inspection rather than relying solely on oral description.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the statutory anchor for objecting to hearsay in oral testimony -- if a witness is testifying about something someone else told them (rather than what they personally saw/heard/perceived), it fails the section 55 direct-evidence test unless it independently qualifies under a specific hearsay exception elsewhere in the Act (e.g., admissions, dying declarations, res gestae). Keep the two provisos in mind as narrow, genuine exceptions -- expert treatises when the expert is unavailable, and the Court's power to call for the physical object itself.

sections.title: Proof of contents of documents
sections.raw_text: 56. The contents of documents may be proved either by primary or by secondary evidence.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter V (Documentary Evidence) with the master division: whatever a document says can be proved in one of two ways -- primary evidence (the document itself) or secondary evidence (a substitute such as a certified copy or oral account). Sections 57-58 define each; sections 59-60 govern when the secondary route is actually allowed.
essential_elements: Document contents can be proved only by primary evidence or secondary evidence -- no third route.
breakdown.how_to_read: A one-line signpost. Read it together with sections 57 (primary evidence defined), 58 (secondary evidence defined), and 59-60 (which one you're allowed to use and when).

sections.title: Primary evidence
sections.raw_text:
57. Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Explanation 1.—Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Explanation 2.—Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart being executed by one or some of the parties only, each counterpart is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Explanation 3.—Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest; but, where they are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Explanation 4.—Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored, and such storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Explanation 5.—Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, such electronic and digital record is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Explanation 6.—Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Explanation 7.—Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
Illustration.
A person is shown to have been in possession of a number of placards, all printed at one time from one original. Any one of the placards is primary evidence of the contents of any other, but no one of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original.

breakdown.plain_summary: Defines primary evidence as the document itself, then extends the concept through seven Explanations. Explanations 1-3 handle multi-part documents, counterparts, and uniformly-produced copies (each is primary evidence of the others, though not of a shared original they were all copied from). Explanations 4-7 -- new relative to the old Evidence Act -- extend the same logic to the digital world: simultaneously or sequentially stored electronic files, records from proper custody, simultaneously stored video recordings, and multiple automated/temporary storage copies are all treated as primary evidence in their own right.
essential_elements: Core definition: the document itself, produced for the Court's inspection.
Explanation 1: each part of a multi-part document is primary evidence.
Explanation 2: each counterpart is primary evidence against the party who executed it.
Explanation 3: each copy from a uniform process (printing/lithography/photography) is primary evidence of the others' contents, but not of a common original they were all copied from.

Explanations 4-7: multiple electronic-record scenarios (simultaneous/sequential multi-file storage, proper-custody records, simultaneously stored video, and automated/temporary storage copies) are each treated as primary evidence.
breakdown.how_to_read: The digital Explanations (4-7) are a deliberate modernisation over the old Evidence Act and matter a great deal in practice -- they mean a forensic image or a server-side copy of a file can itself be primary evidence, not merely secondary evidence of some other 'original', provided the storage/custody conditions in the relevant Explanation are met.

sections.title: Secondary evidence

breakdown.plain_summary: Lists eight categories of secondary evidence -- everything that stands in for the document itself: certified copies, mechanically accurate copies (and copies compared with them), copies made from or compared with the original, counterparts against non-executing parties, oral accounts by an eyewitness to the document, oral and written admissions, and the summarised evidence of a skilled examiner where the originals are too numerous to conveniently examine in Court. The four illustrations draw a careful line: a copy is secondary evidence only if its chain back to the original is actually established -- an oral account of a mere copy, or of a photograph of a copy, is not secondary evidence of the original at all.
essential_elements: Eight categories: certified copies; mechanically-accurate copies and copies compared with them; copies made from/compared with the original; counterparts against non-signing parties; eyewitness oral accounts of the document's contents; oral admissions; written admissions; and skilled-examiner evidence where originals are too numerous to examine.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Illustrations (a)-(d) qualify the list: a copy or account is secondary evidence of the original only where the link back to the original (comparison, photographing the actual original, etc.) is established -- a copy of a copy, or an oral account of a photograph/machine-copy, breaks the chain and is not secondary evidence of the original.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat the eight categories as a checklist when the original is unavailable and you need to fall back to secondary evidence under sections 59-60. But always verify the chain the illustrations describe -- a copy that hasn't actually been compared with or traced to the original does not qualify, however document-like it looks.

sections.title: Proof of documents by primary evidence
sections.raw_text: 59. Documents shall be proved by primary evidence except in the cases hereinafter mentioned.

breakdown.plain_summary: States the default rule plainly: primary evidence (the document itself) is required to prove a document, unless one of the specific exceptions that follow (section 60) applies. Secondary evidence is the exception, not a free alternative.
essential_elements: The general rule is primary evidence.
Secondary evidence is permitted only in the specific cases listed in section 60.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but important framing section -- it establishes that section 60's list is exhaustive, not illustrative. If a case doesn't fit one of section 60's categories, secondary evidence isn't admissible for that document.

sections.title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the operative exceptions list referenced by section 59 -- seven situations (a) to (g) where secondary evidence becomes admissible: the original is with the opposing party, an out-of-reach person, or someone legally bound to produce it (and they don't after notice); its contents are admitted in writing; it's destroyed, lost, or otherwise genuinely unobtainable in time; it's physically immovable; it's a public document; a certified copy is otherwise permitted by law; or the originals are too numerous to conveniently examine and only the general result matters. The Explanation then narrows what kind of secondary evidence is allowed for each category -- for public documents and law-permitted certified-copy documents, only a certified copy will do, not just any secondary evidence.
essential_elements: Seven gateway categories (a)-(g): non-production after notice by a possessing/bound party; written admission of contents; loss/destruction/genuine unavailability; physical immovability; public documents; documents where certified copies are otherwise legally permitted; and numerous-accounts situations needing only a general result.

The Explanation tailors the permitted evidence type per category: clauses (a),(c),(d) allow any secondary evidence; clause (b) allows the written admission itself; clauses (e)/(f) allow ONLY a certified copy, no other secondary evidence; clause (g) allows a skilled examiner's evidence of the general result.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clauses (e) and (f) are a genuine narrowing, not a broadening -- even though the document qualifies for the secondary-evidence route, only a certified copy is admissible for it, other forms of secondary evidence (oral accounts, uncertified copies) will not do.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cross-reference clause (a) with section 64's notice-to-produce procedure -- secondary evidence under clause (a) is only available after that notice has been given and ignored.
