And always check the Explanation before assuming any secondary evidence will do; for public documents and certified-copy-permitted documents, insist on (or expect to have to produce) a certified copy specifically.

sections.title: Admissibility of electronic records
sections.raw_text: 61. Nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record in the evidence on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record and such record shall, subject to section 63, have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as other document.

breakdown.plain_summary: A non-discrimination clause for digital evidence: an electronic or digital record cannot be excluded merely because it is electronic, and it carries the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as any other document -- subject only to meeting section 63's authentication conditions.
essential_elements: Electronic/digital records cannot be denied admissibility solely because of their electronic/digital nature.
They have the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as any other document.
This equal treatment is subject to section 63 -- the authentication conditions there still have to be satisfied.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the foundational 'no discrimination against digital evidence' principle, but don't stop here -- section 63 is where the actual admissibility conditions live, and compliance with it is not optional.

sections.title: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record
sections.raw_text: 62. The contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short bridging section: it directs that proving what an electronic record actually contains is governed specifically by section 63's detailed regime, not by the general primary/secondary evidence rules of sections 56-60.
essential_elements: Proof of the contents of electronic records is governed by section 63.
breakdown.how_to_read: Purely a signpost to section 63 -- the real substance, including the critical certificate requirement, is there.

sections.title: Admissibility of electronic records
sections.raw_text:
63. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory which is produced by a computer or any communication device or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (hereinafter referred to as the computer output) shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question and shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence or any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible.
(2) The conditions referred to in sub-section (1) in respect of a computer output shall be the following, namely:—
(a) the computer output containing the information was produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over the use of the computer or communication device;
(b) during the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived was regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities;
(c) throughout the material part of the said period, the computer or communication device was operating properly or, if not, then in respect of any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period, was not such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and
(d) the information contained in the electronic record reproduces or is derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.
(3) Where over any period, the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period as mentioned in clause (a) of sub-section (2) was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication device, whether—
(a) in standalone mode; or
(b) on a computer system; or
(c) on a computer network; or
(d) on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage; or
(e) through an intermediary,
all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device; and references in this section to a computer or communication device shall be construed accordingly.
(4) In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the following things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely:—
(a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced;
(b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3);
(c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate,
and purporting to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; and for the purposes of this sub-section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.
(5) For the purposes of this section,—
(a) information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment;
(b) a computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).

breakdown.plain_summary: The single most litigated provision in this Chapter -- the successor to the old Evidence Act's section 65B. It deems 'computer output' (any electronic record's information, however printed, stored, or copied) to be a document admissible without producing the original, but only on strict conditions. Subsection (2) sets four reliability conditions: the device was in regular use for the relevant activity, matching information was regularly fed in during that period, the device was working properly (or any malfunction didn't affect accuracy), and the output actually reproduces or derives from the fed-in information. Subsection (3) clarifies that a chain of multiple linked computers/devices (standalone, networked, cloud-resource, or via an intermediary) is treated as one single device for this analysis. Subsection (4) is the operative bottleneck: a signed certificate -- identifying the record, describing the producing device, and addressing the subsection (2) conditions, to the best of the certifier's knowledge and belief -- must accompany the electronic record every time it is tendered. Subsection (5) clarifies that information counts as 'supplied' or 'produced' whether done directly, with human involvement, or through other electronic means.
essential_elements: Subsection (1): computer output is deemed a document, admissible without the original or further proof, IF the section's conditions are met.

Subsection (2): four conditions -- regular use of the device for the relevant activity; regular feeding of matching information during that period; proper (or accuracy-unaffected) operation of the device; and the output reproducing/deriving from the fed-in information.
Subsection (3): multiple computers/devices used in combination (standalone, system, network, cloud resource, or intermediary) are treated as a single device for this analysis.

Subsection (4): a signed certificate identifying the record, the producing device, and addressing the subsection (2) conditions MUST be submitted with the electronic record at every instance of tender; it may be given to the best of the certifier's knowledge and belief, per the format in the Schedule.
Subsection (5): information is 'supplied' or 'produced' whether directly, with human intervention, or through other electronic means -- the human-in-the-loop question doesn't defeat the section.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam' opening makes this a non-obstante provision -- it overrides the general primary/secondary evidence scheme for electronic records specifically.

The subsection (4) certificate is a mandatory precondition to admissibility under this section, not a mere formality -- without it, the computer output cannot be admitted through this route (a point emphasised in Supreme Court jurisprudence on the predecessor provision).
breakdown.how_to_read: The most practice-critical section in the electronic-evidence scheme: always insist on (or prepare) the subsection (4) certificate whenever tendering electronic evidence -- call logs, CCTV footage, WhatsApp chats, server logs, CDRs. Missing or defective certificates are a standard, often fatal, ground of objection. Walk through the four subsection (2) conditions like a checklist when drafting or challenging a certificate, and remember subsection (3)'s single-device fiction when the record passed through a chain of systems or an intermediary.

sections.title: Rules as to notice to produce

breakdown.plain_summary: Fills in the procedural precondition for section 60(a)'s secondary-evidence route: before you can rely on secondary evidence because the opposing party won't produce the original, you must first have given them (or their advocate) notice to produce it -- whatever form of notice the law prescribes, or a reasonable one if none is prescribed. Six situations, plus a residual judicial discretion, dispense with this notice requirement entirely.
essential_elements: General rule: secondary evidence under section 60(a) requires prior notice to produce the original, given to the possessing party, their advocate, or representative.
The notice must follow whatever form is legally prescribed; absent a prescribed form, whatever the Court considers reasonable in the circumstances.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Six proviso exceptions dispense with notice: the document is itself a notice; the adverse party would obviously know production was required; the adverse party obtained the original by fraud or force; the adverse party already has it in Court; the adverse party has admitted its loss; or the possessor is out of the Court's reach.
The Court also has a residual discretion to dispense with notice in any other case it thinks fit.
breakdown.how_to_read: A procedural gatekeeper -- don't assume section 60(a)'s secondary-evidence route is automatically available just because the original is with the other side; check whether notice to produce was actually given, or whether one of the six proviso exceptions (or the Court's residual discretion) applies before relying on it.

sections.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
sections.raw_text: 65. If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.

breakdown.plain_summary: A straightforward proof requirement: if you're relying on a document because a particular person signed or wrote it (wholly or in part), you must actually prove that the signature or handwriting in question genuinely belongs to that person -- it isn't assumed just because the document says so.
essential_elements: Applies whenever a document's signature or handwriting is attributed to a specific person.
That signature/handwriting must be affirmatively proved to be theirs -- covering the full extent alleged to be in their hand, whether the whole document or only part of it.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pairs naturally with section 41 (opinion evidence on handwriting) -- that's typically how this proof is discharged, via a witness acquainted with the handwriting, an expert comparison, or the person's own admission.

sections.title: Proof as to electronic signature
sections.raw_text: 66. Except in the case of a secure electronic signature, if the electronic signature of any subscriber is alleged to have been affixed to an electronic record, the fact that such electronic signature is the electronic signature of the subscriber must be proved.

breakdown.plain_summary: The digital counterpart to section 65: if an electronic record is alleged to bear a particular subscriber's electronic signature, that attribution must be proved -- unless it is a 'secure electronic signature', which is carved out of this proof requirement (because the law separately presumes its reliability).
essential_elements: Applies to any alleged electronic signature of a subscriber affixed to an electronic record.
The link between the signature and the subscriber must be proved.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Carve-out: secure electronic signatures don't need this proof -- their attribution is treated as reliable enough on its own.
breakdown.how_to_read: Mirrors section 65's logic for the digital world -- know the difference between an ordinary electronic signature (attribution must be proved) and a secure electronic signature (exempted from this proof requirement) when assessing what still needs to be established.

sections.title: Proof of execution of document required by law to be attested
sections.raw_text:
67. If a document is required by law to be attested, it shall not be used as evidence until one attesting witness at least has been called for the purpose of proving its execution, if there be an attesting witness alive, and subject to the process of the Court and capable of giving evidence:
Provided that it shall not be necessary to call an attesting witness in proof of the execution of any document, not being a will, which has been registered in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, unless its execution by the person by whom it purports to have been executed is specifically denied.

breakdown.plain_summary: For documents the law requires to be attested (wills, certain deeds), at least one living, reachable, competent attesting witness generally must be called before the document can be used as evidence -- attestation isn't self-proving. The proviso significantly narrows this in practice: for registered documents other than wills, you don't need to call an attesting witness at all, unless the person who supposedly executed it specifically denies having done so.
essential_elements: General rule: a legally-required-to-be-attested document needs at least one attesting witness called to prove execution, IF such a witness is alive, within the Court's reach, and capable of giving evidence.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Proviso: for registered documents (other than wills) under the Indian Registration Act, 1908, no attesting witness needs to be called at all -- unless the purported executant specifically denies executing it.
breakdown.how_to_read: In practice, most registered non-will documents skip the attesting-witness requirement entirely because of the proviso -- reserve the general rule mainly for wills and unregistered attestation-required documents. Watch for a specific denial of execution, which reopens the requirement even for registered documents.

sections.title: Proof where no attesting witness found
sections.raw_text: 68. If no such attesting witness can be found, it must be proved that the attestation of one attesting witness at least is in his handwriting, and that the signature of the person executing the document is in the handwriting of that person.

breakdown.plain_summary: The fallback when section 67's attesting witness cannot be found (or, by extension, isn't alive/reachable/capable): instead of live testimony, you prove the attestation itself is in that witness's handwriting, and separately that the executant's signature is in the executant's own handwriting.
essential_elements: Applies only when no qualifying attesting witness (per section 67) is available.
Requires proving: (1) the attestation is in the handwriting of at least one attesting witness, and (2) the executant's signature is in the executant's own handwriting.
breakdown.how_to_read: A two-part handwriting-proof substitute for live attesting-witness testimony -- both elements are needed, not just one; proving the witness's handwriting alone doesn't establish that the executant actually signed it.

sections.title: Admission of execution by party to attested document
sections.raw_text: 69. The admission of a party to an attested document of its execution by himself shall be sufficient proof of its execution as against him, though it be a document required by law to be attested.

breakdown.plain_summary: A shortcut around the attestation-proof machinery: if the person who executed an attested document simply admits they executed it, that admission alone is sufficient proof of execution against them -- even though the document is legally required to be attested and would otherwise need an attesting witness under section 67.
essential_elements: The admission must come from the party to the attested document, regarding their own execution of it.
That admission is sufficient proof of execution as against that party, overriding the usual attestation-witness requirement.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical shortcut -- if the executant admits execution, don't bother with attesting witnesses at all; the admission binds them directly. But note it only proves execution 'as against him' -- it doesn't necessarily bind other parties to the document.

sections.title: Proof when attesting witness denies execution
sections.raw_text: 70. If the attesting witness denies or does not recollect the execution of the document, its execution may be proved by other evidence.

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes a potential gap: if the attesting witness who was called under section 67 turns hostile (denies execution) or simply can't remember it, that doesn't kill the case -- execution can still be proved through other evidence.
essential_elements: Triggered when a called attesting witness either denies the execution or does not recollect it.
Execution may then be proved by any other evidence, not limited to attesting-witness testimony.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with sections 67-69 as the complete toolkit for proving attested documents: call the witness (67); if unavailable, prove handwriting (68); if the executant admits it, that suffices (69); and if the witness is called but denies or forgets, fall back on other evidence (70).

sections.title: Proof of document not required by law to be attested
sections.raw_text: 71. An attested document not required by law to be attested may be proved as if it was unattested.

breakdown.plain_summary: Clarifies that attestation which happens to appear on a document, but which the law didn't actually require, doesn't trigger sections 67-70's special attesting-witness machinery -- such a document can simply be proved through the ordinary rules, as if it carried no attestation at all.
essential_elements: Applies to documents that are attested in fact, but not required by law to be attested.
Such documents may be proved by ordinary means, ignoring the attestation.
breakdown.how_to_read: A useful distinction to keep straight: attestation only matters procedurally when the law mandates it (section 67). Voluntary or incidental attestation on a document that the law doesn't require to be attested is legally surplus for proof purposes.

sections.title: Comparison of signature, writing or seal with others admitted or proved
sections.raw_text:
72. (1) In order to ascertain whether a signature, writing or seal is that of the person by whom it purports to have been written or made, any signature, writing, or seal admitted or proved to the satisfaction of the Court to have been written or made by that person may be compared with the one which is to be proved, although that signature, writing or seal has not been produced or proved for any other purpose.
(2) The Court may direct any person present in Court to write any words or figures for the purpose of enabling the Court to compare the words or figures so written with any words or figures alleged to have been written by such person.
(3) This section applies also, with any necessary modifications, to finger impressions.

breakdown.plain_summary: Lets a disputed signature, handwriting, seal, or finger impression be checked against a genuine sample -- even if that genuine sample was never otherwise going to be produced in the case. The Court can also make someone write on the spot to get a fresh comparison sample.
essential_elements: The genuine specimen must itself be admitted, or proved to the Court's satisfaction, to be that person's writing/signature/seal.
The disputed item is then compared against the genuine specimen -- by the Court, an expert (section 39), or a witness familiar with the handwriting (section 51).
Sub-section (2) lets the Court order a person present in Court to write specific words/figures then and there, purely to create a comparison sample.
Sub-section (3) extends the whole mechanism to finger impressions, not just signatures and writing.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a court-comparison power, distinct from an expert's opinion under section 39 -- the Court itself may compare, though in practice it will usually be assisted by an expert or a familiar witness. Getting someone to write in open court is a useful tool where no undisputed prior sample exists.

sections.title: Proof as to verification of digital signature

breakdown.plain_summary: The digital analogue of section 72 -- instead of visually comparing handwriting, the Court gets the Digital Signature Certificate produced and has someone apply the public key on it to cryptographically verify whether the digital signature checks out.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to digital signatures (as distinct from broader "electronic signatures").
The Court may direct the alleged signer, the Controller, or the Certifying Authority to produce the Digital Signature Certificate.
The Court may direct any other person to apply the public key on that certificate to verify the signature.
breakdown.how_to_read: Under the Information Technology Act, 2000 scheme, "digital signature" (asymmetric cryptosystem + hash function, certified by a licensed Certifying Authority) is a narrower, more specific category than the general "electronic signature". This section gives the Court a direct verification route for that specific, technically standardised category.

sections.title: Public and private documents
sections.raw_text:
74. (1) The following documents are public documents:—
(a) documents forming the acts, or records of the acts—
(i) of the sovereign authority;
(ii) of official bodies and tribunals; and
(iii) of public officers, legislative, judicial and executive of India or of a foreign country;
(b) public records kept in any State or Union territory of private documents.
(2) All other documents except the documents referred to in sub-section (1) are private.

breakdown.plain_summary: Sorts every document into one of two buckets: public documents (records of acts of government/official bodies/officers, or a public registry's record of a private document) or private documents (everything else). This classification matters because public documents get their own, easier proof route in the sections that follow.
essential_elements: Public documents include: acts/records of the sovereign authority; acts/records of official bodies and tribunals; acts/records of legislative, judicial, and executive public officers, whether of India or a foreign country.
Public documents also include a public record (e.g. a Sub-Registrar's registry) that itself keeps a copy of a private document.
Everything not fitting sub-section (1) is private, by residual definition.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is purely a classification section -- it doesn't itself prescribe how to prove either category. Sections 75-77 give the proof machinery for public documents (certified copies etc.); private documents fall back on the ordinary primary/secondary evidence rules from Chapter V.

sections.title: Certified copies of public documents
sections.raw_text:
75. Every public officer having the custody of a public document, which any person has a right to inspect, shall give that person on demand a copy of it on payment of the legal fees therefor, together with a certificate written at the foot of such copy that it is a true copy of such document or part thereof, as the case may be, and such certificate shall be dated and subscribed by such officer with his name and his official title, and shall be sealed, whenever such officer is authorised by law to make use of a seal; and such copies so certified shall be called certified copies.
Explanation.—Any officer who, by the ordinary course of official duty, is authorised to deliver such copies, shall be deemed to have the custody of such documents within the meaning of this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: Creates the machinery for "certified copies": a custodian public officer must, on demand and payment of fees, hand over a copy of an inspectable public document with a dated, signed (and sealed, where applicable) certificate at the foot confirming it's a true copy.
essential_elements: Applies only to public documents which the requester has a right to inspect.
The officer must supply the copy on demand and payment of legal fees.
The certificate must be at the foot of the copy, dated, and subscribed with the officer's name and official title, and sealed if the officer is authorised to use a seal.
A document satisfying these formalities is what the Adhiniyam calls a "certified copy".
breakdown.how_to_read: The Explanation widens "custody" so that an officer routinely tasked with issuing such copies counts as having custody, even if they aren't the document's original keeper -- important in large record offices where issuing copies is delegated to a specific desk/officer.

sections.title: Proof of documents by production of certified copies
sections.raw_text: 76. Such certified copies may be produced in proof of the contents of the public documents or parts of the public documents of which they purport to be copies.

breakdown.plain_summary: The payoff of section 75: once you have a certified copy, you can simply produce it in court to prove the contents of the underlying public document -- no need to separately establish loss of the original or satisfy the ordinary secondary-evidence conditions.
essential_elements: Only certified copies made under section 75 qualify for this shortcut.
The certified copy proves the contents of the public document (or the certified part of it) it purports to copy.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a standalone, self-sufficient proof route for public documents -- it operates independently of the general primary/secondary evidence hierarchy in sections 57-63.

sections.title: Proof of other official documents

breakdown.plain_summary: Beyond the general certified-copy route of section 75-76, this section gives specific, ready-made proof methods for particular categories of official material -- government orders/notifications, legislative proceedings, gubernatorial/presidential proclamations, foreign government acts, municipal proceedings, and other foreign public documents.
essential_elements: Government Acts/orders/notifications: departmental records certified by the department head, or a document purporting to be government-printed.
Legislative proceedings: journals of the House, published Acts/abstracts, or government-printed copies.
Presidential/Gubernatorial/Administrator proclamations, orders, Regulations: Official Gazette copies or extracts.
Foreign executive Acts/legislative proceedings: authoritative foreign journals, seal-certified copies, or recognition in a Central Act.
Municipal/local body proceedings: copies certified by the legal keeper, or a body-authorised printed book.

Other foreign public documents: original, or a copy certified by the foreign legal keeper plus a Notary Public/Indian Consul/diplomatic agent certificate, plus proof of the document's character under the foreign law.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as a menu of convenient, self-authenticating proof shortcuts for specific document types -- it supplements rather than replaces sections 75-76's general certified-copy mechanism for public documents that don't fit these specific categories.

sections.title: Presumption as to genuineness of certified copies
sections.raw_text:
78. (1) The Court shall presume to be genuine every document purporting to be a certificate, certified copy or other document, which is by law declared to be admissible as evidence of any particular fact and which purports to be duly certified by any officer of the Central Government or of a State Government:
Provided that such document is substantially in the form and purports to be executed in the manner directed by law in that behalf.
(2) The Court shall also presume that any officer by whom any such document purports to be signed or certified, held, when he signed it, the official character which he claims in such paper.

breakdown.plain_summary: A mandatory presumption: a document that on its face is a certificate/certified copy/other document made admissible by law and purporting to be duly certified by a Central or State Government officer must be presumed genuine, provided it's substantially in the legally prescribed form and manner. The Court must also presume the certifying officer actually held the official position he claims.
essential_elements: The document must purport to be a certificate, certified copy, or other document that some law declares admissible as evidence of a particular fact.
It must purport to be duly certified by a Central or State Government officer.
Proviso: it must be substantially in the form and manner directed by law -- a document wildly departing from the prescribed form loses the presumption.
Sub-section (2) separately presumes the certifying officer's claimed official character/capacity at the time of signing.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a "shall presume" (mandatory, though rebuttable) provision -- contrast with the "may presume" (discretionary) presumptions later in this cluster (e.g. sections 82-83, 88-90). The presumption of genuineness saves the proponent from separately proving the officer's signature and authority every time a certified copy is tendered.

sections.title: Presumption as to documents produced as record of evidence, etc.
sections.raw_text:
79. Whenever any document is produced before any Court, purporting to be a record or memorandum of the evidence, or of any part of the evidence, given by a witness in a judicial proceeding or before any officer authorised by law to take such evidence or to be a statement or confession by any prisoner or accused person, taken in accordance with law, and purporting to be signed by any Judge or Magistrate, or by any such officer as aforesaid, the Court shall presume that—
(i) the document is genuine;
(ii) any statements as to the circumstances under which it was taken, purporting to be made by the person signing it, are true; and
(iii) such evidence, statement or confession was duly taken.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a document purports to be a Judge's/Magistrate's/authorised officer's signed record of a witness's evidence, or a prisoner's/accused's statement or confession, the Court must presume three things at once: the record is genuine, any recital of the circumstances of recording is true, and the underlying evidence/statement/confession was duly (i.e. properly) taken.
essential_elements: Applies to records/memoranda of evidence in a judicial proceeding or before a legally authorised officer, and to statements or confessions of a prisoner or accused.
The document must purport to be signed by a Judge, Magistrate, or the authorised officer who took it.
Three simultaneous presumptions follow: genuineness, truth of any recorded circumstances, and due/proper taking of the evidence or statement.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the presumption that gives a properly signed 164-statement-style record (recorded confession/statement, or a deposition) its evidentiary weight without the recording officer needing to separately prove every formality each time it's tendered -- though it remains rebuttable.

sections.title: Presumption as to Gazettes, newspapers, and other documents
sections.raw_text:
80. The Court shall presume the genuineness of every document purporting to be the Official Gazette, or to be a newspaper or journal, and of every document purporting to be a document directed by any law to be kept by any person, if such document is kept substantially in the form required by law and is produced from proper custody.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section and section 92, document is said to be in proper custody if it is in the place in which, and looked after by the person with whom such document is required to be kept; but no custody is improper if it is proved to have had a legitimate origin, or if the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render that origin probable.

breakdown.plain_summary: Extends a genuineness presumption to the Official Gazette, newspapers/journals, and any document that some law requires a particular person to keep -- so long as it's kept substantially in the legally required form and comes from "proper custody" as defined in the Explanation.
essential_elements: Covers three categories: the Official Gazette; newspapers/journals; and law-mandated kept documents.
The document must be substantially in the legally required form.
It must be produced from proper custody -- i.e. the place where, and with the person by whom, it is required to be kept.
The Explanation relaxes this: custody isn't improper merely because it deviates, so long as a legitimate origin is proved or is rendered probable by the circumstances.
breakdown.how_to_read: "Proper custody" as defined here is a recurring concept -- the Explanation is expressly incorporated by reference into section 92 (thirty-year-old documents) as well, so master the definition once and apply it in both places.

sections.title: Presumption as to Gazettes in electronic or digital record
sections.raw_text:
81. The Court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic or digital record purporting to be the Official Gazette, or purporting to be electronic or digital record directed by any law to be kept by any person, if such electronic or digital record is kept substantially in the form required by law and is produced from proper custody.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section and section 93 electronic records are said to be in proper custody if they are in the place in which, and looked after by the person with whom such document is required to be kept; but no custody is improper if it is proved to have had a legitimate origin, or the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render that origin probable.

breakdown.plain_summary: The electronic/digital-record counterpart to section 80 -- an Official Gazette or law-mandated record kept in electronic or digital form gets the same genuineness presumption, on the same substantially-in-form-and-proper-custody conditions.
essential_elements: Covers the Official Gazette and law-mandated records, specifically in electronic or digital record form.
Same two conditions as section 80: substantially the required form, and proper custody.
Its own Explanation on "proper custody" is expressly carried over into section 93 (five-year-old electronic records).
breakdown.how_to_read: BSA consistently pairs a paper-document presumption with a parallel electronic-record presumption (80/81, 92/93) rather than folding electronic records into the same section -- a structural pattern worth noticing across this Chapter.

sections.title: Presumption as to maps or plans made by authority of Government
sections.raw_text: 82. The Court shall presume that maps or plans purporting to be made by the authority of the Central Government or any State Government were so made, and are accurate; but maps or plans made for the purposes of any cause must be proved to be accurate.

breakdown.plain_summary: Maps/plans that purport to be made under Central or State Government authority are presumed both genuine and accurate. But a map/plan specially made for the purposes of the very case at hand doesn't get this free pass -- its accuracy must actually be proved.
essential_elements: Presumption applies to maps/plans purporting to be made under Central/State Government authority.
Covers both genuineness (that it was so made) and accuracy.
Carve-out: maps/plans made specifically for the purposes of a cause (i.e. litigation-generated) must be proved accurate -- no presumption.
breakdown.how_to_read: The litigation-generated-map carve-out guards against a party commissioning a self-serving map and then trying to claim an automatic accuracy presumption for it.

sections.title: Presumption as to collections of laws and reports of decisions
sections.raw_text: 83. The Court shall presume the genuineness of, every book purporting to be printed or published under the authority of the Government of any country, and to contain any of the laws of that country, and of every book purporting to contain reports of decisions of the Courts of such country.

breakdown.plain_summary: Law books and law reports that purport to be government-authorised (for the former) get a genuineness presumption -- useful for proving foreign law and foreign case law without separately authenticating every volume.
essential_elements: Two categories: books purporting to be printed/published under a country's government authority and containing that country's laws; and books purporting to contain that country's court decisions.
Only genuineness is presumed here (unlike section 82's accuracy presumption for government maps).
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is a practical tool in cases involving foreign law or comparative authority -- it removes the need to formally prove the authenticity of the statute book or law report itself before relying on its contents.

sections.title: Presumption as to powers-of-attorney
sections.raw_text: 84. The Court shall presume that every document purporting to be a power-of-attorney, and to have been executed before, and authenticated by, a Notary Public, or any Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul or Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government, was so executed and authenticated.

breakdown.plain_summary: A power-of-attorney that purports to have been executed before, and authenticated by, one of a specified list of authorities (Notary Public, Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul/Vice-Consul, or a Central Government representative) is presumed to have actually been so executed and authenticated.
essential_elements: Applies only to documents purporting to be powers-of-attorney.
The authenticating authority must be one of the specified list -- Notary Public, Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul/Vice-Consul, or Central Government representative.
What's presumed is due execution and authentication, not the underlying content/authority granted by the instrument.
breakdown.how_to_read: This presumption smooths the everyday use of powers-of-attorney (very common in property and commercial transactions) by removing the need to independently prove the formalities of execution before a listed authority.

sections.title: Presumption as to electronic agreements
sections.raw_text: 85. The Court shall presume that every electronic record purporting to be an agreement containing the electronic or digital signature of the parties was so concluded by affixing the electronic or digital signature of the parties.

breakdown.plain_summary: An electronic record that purports to be an agreement bearing the parties' electronic/digital signatures is presumed to have actually been concluded by those parties affixing their signatures.
essential_elements: The electronic record must purport to be an agreement containing the electronic or digital signature of the parties.
What's presumed: the agreement was concluded through the parties affixing their electronic/digital signatures.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the electronic-contracting counterpart to the presumption of due execution that attaches to a conventionally signed agreement -- it supports the enforceability of e-contracts and click-wrap/digitally-signed agreements.

sections.title: Presumption as to electronic records and electronic signatures
sections.raw_text:
86. (1) In any proceeding involving a secure electronic record, the Court shall presume unless contrary is proved, that the secure electronic record has not been altered since the specific point of time to which the secure status relates.
(2) In any proceeding, involving secure electronic signature, the Court shall presume unless the contrary is proved that—
(a) the secure electronic signature is affixed by subscriber with the intention of signing or approving the electronic record;
(b) except in the case of a secure electronic record or a secure electronic signature, nothing in this section shall create any presumption, relating to authenticity and integrity of the electronic record or any electronic signature.

breakdown.plain_summary: Confers strong, though rebuttable, presumptions specifically on "secure" electronic records and "secure" electronic signatures (as opposed to ordinary electronic records/signatures): a secure record is presumed unaltered since it attained secure status, and a secure signature is presumed affixed by the subscriber with intent to sign/approve. Clause (b) is a clarifying carve-out that this special presumption doesn't extend to ordinary (non-secure) electronic records or signatures.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): applies only to a "secure electronic record" -- presumed unaltered since the point in time its secure status attached, unless the contrary is proved.
Sub-section (2)(a): applies only to a "secure electronic signature" -- presumed affixed by the subscriber with intent to sign/approve, unless the contrary is proved.
Sub-section (2)(b): no equivalent presumption of authenticity/integrity arises for electronic records or signatures that are not "secure" in the technical sense.
breakdown.how_to_read: "Secure electronic record" and "secure electronic signature" are technical terms of art from the Information Technology Act, 2000 framework (tied to specific security procedures), distinct from an ordinary electronic signature under section 66-67. Don't assume every digitally signed document is automatically "secure" in this heightened sense.

sections.title: Presumption as to Electronic Signature Certificates
sections.raw_text: 87. The Court shall presume, unless contrary is proved, that the information listed in an Electronic Signature Certificate is correct, except for information specified as subscriber information which has not been verified, if the certificate was accepted by the subscriber.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a subscriber has accepted an Electronic Signature Certificate, the Court presumes the information listed on it is correct -- except for any information flagged on the certificate itself as unverified subscriber information, which gets no such presumption.
essential_elements: Precondition: the certificate must have been accepted by the subscriber.
General rule: information listed on the certificate is presumed correct, rebuttably.
Carve-out: information specifically marked as unverified subscriber information is excluded from the presumption.
breakdown.how_to_read: This presumption is what makes Electronic Signature Certificates practically usable in court -- without it, every detail on the certificate would need independent proof each time.

sections.title: Presumption as to certified copies of foreign judicial records
sections.raw_text:
88. (1) The Court may presume that any document purporting to be a certified copy of any judicial record of any country beyond India is genuine and accurate, if the document purports to be certified in any manner which is certified by any representative of the Central Government in or for such country to be the manner commonly in use in that country for the certification of copies of judicial records.
(2) An officer who, with respect to any territory or place outside India is a Political Agent therefor, as defined in clause (43) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall, for the purposes of this section, be deemed to be a representative of the Central Government in and for the country comprising that territory or place.

breakdown.plain_summary: A discretionary ("may presume") presumption of genuineness and accuracy for certified copies of foreign judicial records, provided the certification method is itself certified by a Central Government representative in that country as the commonly used method there.
essential_elements: Applies to certified copies of judicial records of a country outside India.
The certification manner must itself be certified, by a Central Government representative in/for that country, as the manner commonly in use there.
Discretionary presumption ("may presume") -- the Court is not bound to presume, unlike section 78's "shall presume".
Sub-section (2) deems a Political Agent (as defined in the General Clauses Act, 1897) to be such a Central Government representative for this purpose.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the deliberate shift from "shall presume" (sections 78-81, mandatory) to "may presume" (this section onward through 90) -- foreign-sourced documents get a more cautious, discretionary treatment than domestic government-certified ones.

sections.title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts
sections.raw_text: 89. The Court may presume that any book to which it may refer for information on matters of public or general interest, and that any published map or chart, the statements of which are relevant facts, and which is produced for its inspection, was written and published by the person, and at the time and place, by whom or at which it purports to have been written or published.

breakdown.plain_summary: A discretionary presumption covering reference books on matters of public/general interest, and published maps/charts whose statements are relevant -- the Court may presume they were written/published by the person, and at the time and place, they purport to have been.
essential_elements: Two categories: (a) books the Court may refer to for information on matters of public or general interest; (b) published maps/charts whose statements are relevant facts.
The book/map/chart must be produced for the Court's inspection.
The presumption covers authorship/publication attribution -- who published it, and when and where.
breakdown.how_to_read: This overlaps functionally with judicial notice (section 52) for well-known reference works, but operates as a document-specific evidentiary presumption rather than dispensing with proof altogether.

sections.title: Presumption as to electronic messages
sections.raw_text: 90. The Court may presume that an electronic message, forwarded by the originator through an electronic mail server to the addressee to whom the message purports to be addressed corresponds with the message as fed into his computer for transmission; but the Court shall not make any presumption as to the person by whom such message was sent.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court may presume that an email, as received by the addressee, matches what the originator actually typed/fed into the computer for sending -- but this presumption stops at message-integrity; it does not extend to who actually sent it.
essential_elements: Applies to an electronic message forwarded by the originator through a mail server to the addressee it purports to be addressed to.
Presumption covers only correspondence between the sent version and the received version (transmission integrity).
Express bar: no presumption arises as to the identity of the person who actually sent the message.
breakdown.how_to_read: The identity carve-out is deliberate and important -- email accounts can be spoofed, shared, or compromised, so BSA declines to presume that the named originator was the actual human who sent it; that must be independently proved.

sections.title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced
sections.raw_text: 91. The Court shall presume that every document, called for and not produced after notice to produce, was attested, stamped and executed in the manner required by law.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a party is given notice to produce a document (the section 64 mechanism) and fails to produce it, the Court must presume that the document -- whatever it said -- was properly attested, stamped, and executed as the law requires.
essential_elements: Applies where a document was called for (i.e. notice to produce was given) and not produced.
Mandatory presumption ("shall presume") of due attestation, stamping, and execution.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a penalty-style presumption against the non-producing party -- it works alongside section 64 (notice to produce triggering secondary evidence) and section 167 (barring later use of a document whose production was earlier refused), together discouraging strategic withholding of documents.

sections.title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old
sections.raw_text:
92. Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting, and, in the case of a document executed or attested, that it was duly executed and attested by the persons by whom it purports to be executed and attested.
Explanation.—The Explanation to section 80 shall also apply to this section.
Illustrations.
(a) A has been in possession of landed property for a long time. He produces from his custody deeds relating to the land showing his titles to it. The custody shall be proper.
(b) A produces deeds relating to landed property of which he is the mortgagee. The mortgagor is in possession. The custody shall be proper.
(c) A, a connection of B, produces deeds relating to lands in B's possession, which were deposited with him by B for safe custody. The custody shall be proper.

breakdown.plain_summary: The classic "thirty-year-old document" presumption: a document that is (or purports to be) thirty years old, produced from custody the Court considers proper in the circumstances, may be presumed to be in the handwriting it purports to be in, and, if it purports to be executed/attested, to have been duly executed and attested.
essential_elements: The document must purport, or be proved, to be thirty years old.
It must be produced from custody the Court considers proper in the particular case -- "proper custody" borrows section 80's Explanation.
Presumption covers handwriting attribution and, for executed/attested documents, due execution and attestation.
Discretionary ("may presume"), not mandatory.

The Illustrations show "proper custody" is interpreted flexibly -- a title-holder's own possession, a mortgagee's possession while the mortgagor holds the land, or a relative's safe-custody holding, are all proper.
breakdown.how_to_read: This presumption is a major practical tool in title/property litigation involving old deeds where the original executants and attesting witnesses are long dead and direct proof of execution is impossible -- age plus proper custody substitutes for that proof.

sections.title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old
sections.raw_text:
93. Where any electronic record, purporting or proved to be five years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that the electronic signature which purports to be the electronic signature of any particular person was so affixed by him or any person authorised by him in this behalf.
Explanation.—The Explanation to section 81 shall also apply to this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: The electronic-record counterpart to section 92's thirty-year presumption, but with a much shorter threshold (five years) reflecting how quickly electronic records age and turn over -- an electronic signature on a five-year-old record from proper custody may be presumed affixed by the person it purports to be, or someone they authorised.
essential_elements: The electronic record must purport, or be proved, to be five years old.
It must be produced from custody the Court considers proper -- borrowing section 81's proper-custody Explanation.
Presumption covers the electronic signature's attribution to the purported signer or their authorised delegate.
Discretionary ("may presume").
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the much shorter five-year threshold compared to section 92's thirty years -- a deliberate recognition that electronic records and their custodial systems don't have the same multi-generational lifespan as paper deeds.

sections.title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document
sections.raw_text:
94. When the terms of a contract, or of a grant, or of any other disposition of property, have been reduced to the form of a document, and in all cases in which any matter is required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such contract, grant or other disposition of property, or of such matter, except the document itself, or secondary evidence of its contents in cases in which secondary evidence is admissible under the provisions hereinbefore contained.
Exception 1.—When a public officer is required by law to be appointed in writing, and when it is shown that any particular person has acted as such officer, the writing by which he is appointed need not be proved.
Exception 2.—Wills admitted to probate in India may be proved by the probate.
Explanation 1.—This section applies equally to cases in which the contracts, grants or dispositions of property referred to are contained in one document, and to cases in which they are contained in more documents than one.
Explanation 2.—Where there are more originals than one, one original only need be proved.
Explanation 3.—The statement, in any document whatever, of a fact other than the facts referred to in this section, shall not preclude the admission of oral evidence as to the same fact.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter VI's "best evidence" regime: once a contract, grant, or other disposition of property has been put into a document -- or wherever the law requires something to be documented -- the document itself (or admissible secondary evidence of it) is the only way to prove its terms. Oral evidence of what the document said is shut out.
essential_elements: Applies where contract/grant/property-disposition terms have been reduced to a document, or any matter is legally required to be documented.
Only the document itself, or secondary evidence admissible under the earlier sections (57-63), may prove the terms.
Exception 1: where a public officer's appointment must be in writing, and someone has actually acted in that office, the appointment writing itself need not be proved.
Exception 2: probated wills may be proved by the probate.
Explanation 1: applies whether the terms are in one document or spread across several.
Explanation 2: where several originals exist (e.g. counterparts), proving just one suffices.

Explanation 3: a document's incidental recital of some unrelated fact doesn't block oral evidence of that unrelated fact -- the exclusion is narrowly about the contract/grant/disposition terms themselves.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section works hand-in-hand with section 95 -- section 94 says you must prove the document (not orally recreate its terms); section 95 says that once proved, you generally can't contradict/vary it with oral evidence either. Together they form the classic parol evidence rule.

sections.title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement
sections.raw_text:
95. When the terms of any such contract, grant or other disposition of property, or any matter required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, have been proved according to section 94, no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted, as between the parties to any such instrument or their representatives in interest, for the purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to, or subtracting from, its terms:
Provided that any fact may be proved which would invalidate any document, or which would entitle any person to any decree or order relating thereto; such as fraud, intimidation, illegality, want of due execution, want of capacity in any contracting party, want or failure of consideration, or mistake in fact or law:
Provided further that the existence of any separate oral agreement as to any matter on which a document is silent, and which is not inconsistent with its terms, may be proved. In considering whether or not this proviso applies, the Court shall have regard to the degree of formality of the document:
Provided also that the existence of any separate oral agreement, constituting a condition precedent to the attaching of any obligation under any such contract, grant or disposition of property, may be proved:
Provided also that the existence of any distinct subsequent oral agreement to rescind or modify any such contract, grant or disposition of property, may be proved, except in cases in which such contract, grant or disposition of property is by law required to be in writing, or has been registered according to the law in force for the time being as to the registration of documents:
Provided also that any usage or custom by which incidents not expressly mentioned in any contract are usually annexed to contracts of that description, may be proved:
Provided also that the annexing of such incident would not be repugnant to, or inconsistent with, the express terms of the contract:
Provided also that any fact may be proved which shows in what manner the language of a document is related to existing facts.

breakdown.plain_summary: The core parol evidence rule: once a document's terms are proved under section 94, the parties to it (or their representatives) cannot use oral evidence to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from those terms. But this bar comes with six significant carve-outs listed as provisos.
essential_elements: General bar: no oral agreement/statement admissible to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from proved document terms, as between the parties/their representatives in interest.
Proviso 1: facts invalidating the document (fraud, intimidation, illegality, want of due execution, incapacity, failure of consideration, mistake) remain provable.
Proviso 2: a separate oral agreement on a matter the document is silent about, and not inconsistent with it, may be proved -- degree of formality of the document is a relevant factor.
Proviso 3: a separate oral agreement operating as a condition precedent to the obligation attaching may be proved.
Proviso 4: a distinct subsequent oral agreement to rescind or modify may be proved -- except where the instrument is legally required to be in writing or has been registered.
Proviso 5 & 6: usage/custom annexing unstated incidents to contracts of that description may be proved, provided it isn't repugnant to the document's express terms.
Proviso 7 (final): facts showing how the document's language relates to existing facts (i.e. facts needed to apply the document) remain provable.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The registered/required-to-be-in-writing carve-out inside proviso 4 is a frequent litigation flashpoint -- oral rescission/modification of a registered sale deed or lease cannot be proved even under this proviso.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as: general bar, then work through the provisos as recognised exceptions -- vitiating facts, silence-filling collateral agreements, conditions precedent, subsequent rescission/variation (subject to the writing/registration carve-out), usage/custom, and application-to-facts evidence. This is one of the most litigated sections in evidence law -- know each proviso by its function, not just its number.

sections.title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document
sections.raw_text:
96. When the language used in a document is, on its face, ambiguous or defective, evidence may not be given of facts which would show its meaning or supply its defects.
Illustrations.
(a) A agrees, in writing, to sell a horse to B for "one lakh rupees or one lakh fifty thousand rupees". Evidence cannot be given to show which price was to be given.
(b) A deed contains blanks. Evidence cannot be given of facts which would show how they were meant to be filled.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a document is ambiguous or defective on its own face (a "patent" ambiguity, visible without looking outside the document), extrinsic evidence cannot be used to clear it up or fill the gap -- the document simply fails for uncertainty as to that term.
essential_elements: Applies only to ambiguity/defect apparent on the face of the document itself.
No evidence of outside facts is admissible to resolve the ambiguity or supply the missing content.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast this with sections 97-101, which deal with ambiguity that only emerges when the document is applied to the facts ("latent" ambiguity) -- there, extrinsic evidence IS admissible. Section 96 is specifically about ambiguity visible on the document's face alone.

sections.title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts
sections.raw_text:
97. When language used in a document is plain in itself, and when it applies accurately to existing facts, evidence may not be given to show that it was not meant to apply to such facts.
Illustration.
A sells to B, by deed, "my estate at Rampur containing one hundred bighas". A has an estate at Rampur containing one hundred bighas. Evidence may not be given of the fact that the estate meant to be sold was one situated at a different place and of a different size.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a document's plain language accurately matches an existing set of facts, no evidence is admissible to claim the document actually meant something else -- plain language that fits is taken at face value.
essential_elements: Applies where the language is plain in itself and accurately applies to existing facts.
Bars evidence attempting to show the plain, fitting language was meant to apply to something different.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the flip side of section 98 -- section 97 deals with language that fits the facts perfectly (no extrinsic evidence allowed to unsettle it); section 98 deals with language that is plain but doesn't fit any existing fact (extrinsic evidence allowed to find its peculiar sense).

sections.title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts
sections.raw_text:
98. When language used in a document is plain in itself, but is unmeaning in reference to existing facts, evidence may be given to show that it was used in a peculiar sense.
Illustration.
A sells to B, by deed, "my house in Kolkata". A had no house in Kolkata, but it appears that he had a house at Howrah, of which B had been in possession since the execution of the deed. These facts may be proved to show that the deed related to the house at Howrah.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a document's plain language, though clear in itself, simply doesn't correspond to any existing fact (there is no such thing to which it could refer, literally), evidence is admissible to show the words were actually used in some special or peculiar sense that does fit the facts.
essential_elements: Applies where language is plain in itself but unmeaning -- doesn't correspond to any existing fact -- when applied literally.
Evidence is admissible to show a peculiar/special sense in which the words were actually used.
breakdown.how_to_read: The Illustration is the classic example: literal language ("house in Kolkata") that describes nothing that exists opens the door to evidence showing what was really meant (the Howrah house), based on surrounding conduct like possession.

sections.title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons
sections.raw_text:
99. When the facts are such that the language used might have been meant to apply to any one, and could not have been meant to apply to more than one, of several persons or things, evidence may be given of facts which show which of those persons or things it was intended to apply to.
Illustrations.
(a) A agrees to sell to B, for one thousand rupees, "my white horse". A has two white horses. Evidence may be given of facts which show which of them was meant.
(b) A agrees to accompany B to Ramgarh. Evidence may be given of facts showing whether Ramgarh in Rajasthan or Ramgarh in Uttarakhand was meant.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where document language could fit any one, but not more than one, of several possible persons/things, extrinsic evidence is admissible to identify which specific one was actually intended.
essential_elements: Applies where the language could apply to any single one, but not simultaneously to more than one, of several candidates.
Evidence is admissible to pin down which particular person/thing was meant.
breakdown.how_to_read: Classic latent-ambiguity scenario -- "my white horse" is perfectly plain until you discover the seller owns two; extrinsic facts (which horse was shown, discussed, etc.) resolve which one the words point to.

sections.title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies
sections.raw_text:
100. When the language used applies partly to one set of existing facts, and partly to another set of existing facts, but the whole of it does not apply correctly to either, evidence may be given to show to which of the two it was meant to apply.
Illustration.
A agrees to sell to B "my land at X in the occupation of Y". A has land at X, but not in the occupation of Y, and he has land in the occupation of Y but it is not at X. Evidence may be given of facts showing which he meant to sell.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a document's description is split between two possible referents -- partly matching one, partly matching another, but wholly matching neither -- evidence is admissible to determine which one was actually meant.
essential_elements: Applies where language partly fits one set of facts and partly fits a different set, but fully fits neither.
Evidence is admissible to determine the intended referent.
breakdown.how_to_read: The Illustration shows a description split across two properties (right location/wrong occupier vs. wrong location/right occupier) -- neither matches the full description, so extrinsic evidence decides which one the parties meant.

sections.title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc.
sections.raw_text:
101. Evidence may be given to show the meaning of illegible or not commonly intelligible characters, of foreign, obsolete, technical, local and regional expressions, of abbreviations and of words used in a peculiar sense.
Illustration.
A, sculptor, agrees to sell to B, "all my mods". A has both models and modelling tools. Evidence may be given to show which he meant to sell.

breakdown.plain_summary: Extrinsic evidence is admissible to decode illegible writing, uncommon characters, foreign/obsolete/technical/local/regional expressions, abbreviations, and words used in a special sense -- essentially a translation/decoding gateway, not a rule about contested meaning of otherwise-clear language.
essential_elements: Covers: illegible or not commonly intelligible characters; foreign, obsolete, technical, local, and regional expressions; abbreviations; and peculiarly used words.
Evidence (e.g. expert or trade-usage testimony) is admissible to establish what such characters/expressions/abbreviations/words mean.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes out the run of sections 96-101, which collectively map out exactly when extrinsic evidence can and cannot be used to interpret a document -- barred for patent, face-of-document ambiguity (s.96), but allowed for the various latent-ambiguity and decoding scenarios (s.97-101).

sections.title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document
sections.raw_text:
102. Persons who are not parties to a document, or their representatives in interest, may give evidence of any facts tending to show a contemporaneous agreement varying the terms of the document.
Illustration.
A and B make a contract in writing that B shall sell A certain cotton, to be paid for on delivery. At the same time, they make an oral agreement that three months' credit shall be given to A. This could not be shown as between A and B, but it might be shown by C, if it affected his interests.

breakdown.plain_summary: The parol evidence exclusion in sections 94-95 only binds the actual parties to a document (and their representatives in interest) -- a stranger to the document whose own interests are affected may still lead evidence of a contemporaneous oral agreement varying its terms.
essential_elements: Applies to persons who are not parties to the document, or their representatives in interest.
Such persons may prove facts showing a contemporaneous oral agreement varying the document's terms.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the privity limit on the parol evidence rule -- sections 94/95's bar is specifically "as between the parties to any such instrument or their representatives in interest"; a third party whose rights are affected by the document is not bound by that restriction.

sections.title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills
sections.raw_text: 103. Nothing in this Chapter shall be taken to affect any of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925) as to the construction of wills.

breakdown.plain_summary: A savings clause: nothing in Chapter VI (sections 94-102) overrides the Indian Succession Act, 1925's own special rules for construing wills -- will-construction continues to be governed by that Act.
essential_elements: Closes Chapter VI.
Preserves the Indian Succession Act, 1925's provisions on construction of wills, unaffected by this Chapter's document-interpretation rules.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but important carve-out -- wills have their own specialised body of construction rules under succession law, and this section makes clear Chapter VI's general document-interpretation framework doesn't displace them.

sections.title: Burden of proof
sections.raw_text:
104. Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist, and when a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person.
Illustrations.
(a) A desires a Court to give judgment that B shall be punished for a crime which A says B has committed. A must prove that B has committed the crime.
(b) A desires a Court to give judgment that he is entitled to certain land in the possession of B, by reason of facts which he asserts, and which B denies, to be true. A must prove the existence of those facts.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter VII with the foundational definition: whoever wants a Court to grant a judgment based on asserted facts must prove those facts -- that obligation to prove is what "burden of proof" means.
essential_elements: Applies to anyone desiring a judgment on a legal right/liability that depends on asserted facts.
That person must prove the facts they assert.
Definitional: being "bound to prove" a fact is what it means for the burden of proof to lie on someone.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the general, abstract definition; sections 105 onward operationalise it with more specific, practical rules about exactly whom the burden falls on in particular scenarios.

sections.title: On whom burden of proof lies
sections.raw_text:
105. The burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.
Illustrations.
(a) A sues B for land of which B is in possession, and which, as A asserts, was left to A by the will of C, B's father. If no evidence were given on either side, B would be entitled to retain his possession. Therefore, the burden of proof is on A.
(b) A sues B for money due on a bond. The execution of the bond is admitted, but B says that it was obtained by fraud, which A denies. If no evidence were given on either side, A would succeed, as the bond is not disputed and the fraud is not proved. Therefore, the burden of proof is on B.

breakdown.plain_summary: Gives the practical test for locating the overall burden in a suit/proceeding: ask who would lose if absolutely no evidence were led by either side -- that person carries the burden of proof.
essential_elements: The test: who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.
Illustration (a): a possessor-defendant wins by default, so the burden is on the claimant asserting a competing right.
Illustration (b): an admitted, undisputed bond means the plaintiff would win by default, so the burden of proving the fraud defence shifts to the defendant.
breakdown.how_to_read: This "who loses by default" test is the practical operationalisation of section 104's abstract definition, and is frequently invoked in pleadings-stage arguments about which side must lead evidence first.

sections.title: Burden of proof as to particular fact
sections.raw_text:
106. The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on that person who wishes the Court to believe in its existence, unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on any particular person.
Illustration.
A prosecutes B for theft, and wishes the Court to believe that B admitted the theft to C. A must prove the admission. B wishes the Court to believe that, at the time in question, he was elsewhere. He must prove it.

breakdown.plain_summary: Beyond the overall suit-level burden (section 105), each individual particular fact has its own burden: whoever wants the Court to believe that specific fact exists must prove it -- unless some other law specifically assigns that fact's proof to someone else.
essential_elements: Default rule: the burden of any particular fact lies on the person who wants the Court to believe it.
Overridden wherever another law specifically allocates proof of that fact to a particular person.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 105 and 106 operate at different levels of granularity -- 105 identifies who bears the ultimate, overall burden of the case; 106 governs shifting, fact-by-fact burdens for individual assertions within that case (e.g. an alibi, as in the Illustration).

sections.title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible
sections.raw_text:
107. The burden of proving any fact necessary to be proved in order to enable any person to give evidence of any other fact is on the person who wishes to give such evidence.
Illustrations.
(a) A wishes to prove a dying declaration by B. A must prove B's death.
(b) A wishes to prove, by secondary evidence, the contents of a lost document. A must prove that the document has been lost.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where some "gateway fact" must be established before other evidence becomes admissible at all (e.g. proving a declarant is dead before their dying declaration can be led, or proving a document is lost before secondary evidence of it can be led), the burden of proving that gateway fact is on whoever wants to lead the dependent evidence.
essential_elements: Applies to facts that are preconditions for the admissibility of other evidence.
The burden of proving the precondition falls on the party wishing to lead the evidence that depends on it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This connects directly to section 141(2) later in the Adhiniyam, which requires such foundational facts to be proved before the dependent evidence is admitted -- section 107 tells you who carries that foundational burden.

sections.title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions
sections.raw_text:
108. When a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the General Exceptions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or within any special exception or proviso contained in any other part of the said Sanhita, or in any law defining the offence, is upon him, and the Court shall presume the absence of such circumstances.
Illustrations.
(a) A, accused of murder, alleges that, by reason of unsoundness of mind, he did not know the nature of the act. The burden of proof is on A.
(b) A, accused of murder, alleges that, by grave and sudden provocation, he was deprived of the power of self-control. The burden of proof is on A.
(c) Section 117 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 provides that whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (2) of section 122, voluntarily causes grievous hurt, shall be subject to certain punishments. A is charged with voluntarily causing grievous hurt under section 117. The burden of proving the circumstances bringing the case under sub-section (2) of section 122 lies on A.

breakdown.plain_summary: In a criminal case, if the accused wants to rely on a General Exception (like unsoundness of mind or grave and sudden provocation) or any special exception/proviso in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or the law defining the offence, the burden of proving those exculpatory circumstances is on the accused -- and the Court must otherwise presume such circumstances are absent.
essential_elements: Applies to General Exceptions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and to special exceptions/provisos in the BNS or the offence-defining law.
The accused bears the burden of proving facts bringing the case within such an exception.
